1.1: 1.1 Prologue. The Gospel excels all the pages of divine Scripture, because what the law and the prophets foretold would come, the Gospel declares fulfilled. Among the writers of the gospels themselves, John stands out in the profundity of the divine mysteries; from the time of the Lord's Ascension, for sixty-five years, he preached the word of God without the aid of writing, until the last days of Domitian. But when Domitian was killed and, with Nerva's permission, he had returned from exile to Ephesus, he was compelled by the bishops of Asia to write on the divinity of Christ, coeternal with the Father, against the heretics who, in his absence, had burst into his churches and denied that Christ existed before Mary. Hence he is rightly compared, in the figure of the four living creatures, to the flying eagle, which flies higher than the other animals and gazes at the rays of the sun with unblinking eyes. For the other evangelists, who sufficiently set forth the temporal birth of Christ and his temporal deeds which he did in the man, and said little of the divinity, walk with the Lord on earth like creatures that go on foot. But this one, explaining little of his temporal deeds, yet contemplating more sublimely the power of the divinity, flies with the Lord to heaven. For he who lay upon the breast of the Lord at the supper drank the draught of heavenly wisdom more excellently than the others from the very fountain of the Lord's breast. He had read, indeed, the gospels of the three evangelists, and had approved their faith and truth; and he saw that some things in the history of the deeds were lacking, especially what the Lord did in the first time of his preaching, that is, before John the Baptist was shut up in prison. These things, therefore, as if passed over by them, John writes, namely what Jesus did before John was delivered up; but above all he took care to commend the divinity of Christ and the mystery of the Trinity. For the other three evangelists, having followed more copiously the temporal sayings and deeds of the Lord, which are most valuable for forming the morals of the present life, were occupied with the active life. In it one labors that the heart may be cleansed to see God. John, however, relates few deeds of the Lord, but writes down more diligently the words of the Lord that suggest the unity of the Trinity and the happiness of eternal life; and thus he held his intention and preaching on commending virtue in the contemplative life. In it one is free for leisure that God may be seen. This, indeed, is the John whom the Lord called from the tossing storm of the wedding, and to whom he commended his virgin mother, himself a virgin. In the beginning was the Word. Against those who, on account of the temporal birth of Christ, said that Christ had not always been, he begins with the eternity of the Word, saying: In the beginning was the Word.
1.3: 1.3 All things were made by him. AUG. He through whom every creature was made is not a creature, etc., up to with which all agree concerning the power of the Divinity. And without him was made nothing. ORIG. He punctuates thus: And without him was made nothing. The order: There is nothing that was made without him.
1.4: 1.4 That which was made, in him was life. AUG. John Chrysostom: And without him was made nothing. That which was made. Hilary: Without him was made nothing, that which was made in him.
1.6: 1.6 There was a man sent. After he ascended on sublime flight beyond all nature to the height of theology, since he had contemplated that the Word was always with the Father, he soon descends to the humility of human nature, and especially to the forerunner of the Word, against those who said that human nature was wholly lost in the first parent and reduced to nothing. A man sent. A man, not an angel, as the heretics want, sent by God. Therefore he could say of God.
1.9: 1.9 That was the true light. Every man means that nature in man which was made to the image and likeness of God. All other things that are in man are lower parts of man, and in a way are outside man. In that nature, namely the soul, as in a kind of higher world, the true light shines, and enlightens those coming into that world and being born again by grace, because those whose life and conversation is in heaven are as if in another world.
1.11: 1.11 And his own received him not. From the beginning of the world there was no time in which there were not receivers of the divine word, hence he adds: But as many as received him.
1.12: 1.12 To become the sons of God. A wonderful power, that those who were sons of the devil are said, delivered through him, to be both sons of God and brothers of Christ; but in what order they become sons of God, and how this generation differs from the carnal, is added: Who are born not of blood.
1.14: 1.14 And the Word was made flesh. That we may securely believe that men are born of God, he adds that God is born of man; by this taking up of infirmity our infirmity is healed, that we may be able to become sons of God. And this is: And the Word was made flesh. What was above came down below. What wonder if what was below ascends to that which is above? And it is no wonder if men are born of God, because God was born of man. Full of grace and truth. The man Christ was full of grace, because, with no preceding merits, from the moment he was conceived the Deity was in him, filling that man with all fullness, overflowing into all the saints; hence his mother also is called not only mother of a man, but also mother of God. Nor is it a wonder if the man is also called God, when God is also called man; and this is called grace and truth, because it was so promised long ago, and now shown, namely that God be in man, filling him with every good, and through him his own.
1.15: 1.15 This was he of whom I said. By the demonstrative pronoun it is intimated that Christ was present in that place. For often the Lord himself, still unknown, before he was baptized and preached, used to come to John. He that shall come after me. Who, after me born, after me will preach, baptize, die. Not that he was not yet born when he said this, since he had even been baptized: but he is to come in preaching, in death, but not in resurrection. Is preferred before me, because he was before me. From the Greek, he was made before me, that is, he appeared to me indeed, namely because he was before me.
1.16: 1.16 And of his fulness. Having set out the testimony of the forerunner, the evangelist returns to the testimony of his own assertion. As if he said: The Word was made flesh: we saw his glory full of grace and truth, and of his fulness we all have received. Grace, that we may believe him, and truth by which we may understand him. We have received. AUG. Not only grace, which is plainly given freely, not for merit, such as faith which works by love, by which the just man lives, but for this, grace, that is, eternal beatitude, which is also called the reward of justice, and also grace, because merit is from grace. Grace for grace. Grace is given in the conceiving of the good through grace. Grace simply, which is not of merit; if afterwards we work with it and grow accustomed to good things, then grace is given for the former grace.
1.17: 1.17 By Moses. By Moses the servant, the announcement; by the Lord Jesus, the fulfillment of salvation.
1.18: 1.18 No man hath seen God at any time. That is, no mere man living in this body has seen God as he is, hence it was said to Moses: Man shall not see me and live Exod. 33., that is, no one living in the body shall see my divinity. Hence God added this to Moses: Stand in the hole of the rock, and when I shall pass, you shall see my back parts Ibid.. The rock, that is, Christ; the hole, the gibbet of the cross; when I shall pass, that is, when I shall pass from the world to the Father. The back parts: his rising, passion, resurrection, ascension, by which, being believed, we come to his beatitude and vision. That we read that God appeared to men, whether visibly to carnal eyes, or invisibly in prophetic visions through a subject creature, is to be understood thus: the visions of the prophets were made through some spiritual creature, by which they are said to have seen God. The only begotten Son, etc. What is the sum of grace and truth he briefly adds, namely the knowledge of the Trinity itself, hence: This is eternal life, that they may know thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent. This is not full in this life, because no one in the flesh has seen God as he is. Hence not even Moses himself, much less was grace given through him, as even he himself after all he had seen in the type of God said: Show me thyself Exod. 33., but the Son, who is in the secret of the Father, has declared him, because no one knoweth the Father but the Son, and he to whom it shall please the Son to reveal him Luc. 10.. He himself tells his own what is to be thought of the Trinity of the deity, how to arrive at it, and he introduces them to it.
1.19: 1.19 And this. And these and the other following testimonies of John were given after Christ was baptized, when Jesus was already coming to invite the disciples, whom John by his testimonies sends to him. Testimony against the notion that Christ is hidden: hidden because humble: humble so that he could be despised and killed, to redeem the world. Who art thou? The Jews thought John to be the Christ, who was promised in the law. Others thought him to be Elias, on account of his great abstinence and chastity, and solitary life, and most severe reproof of sins, and the harshest terror of future vengeance. Others said he was one of the prophets risen again, on account of the grace of prophecy.
1.20: 1.20 He confessed. He confessed, as he afterwards says, that he was not the Christ. He did not deny what he was, that is, that he was the forerunner, as when asked afterwards he says: I am the voice of one crying. The order of the words: and he confessed and did not deny, when they sent.
1.21: 1.21 Art thou Elias? Though all knew the name of Christ, they also knew that Elias would go before him. But Elias himself is to go before the one who will judge in power; John is figuratively Elias for the same one who is to be judged, so that there may be two heralds as there are two comings of the same: hence: I am not Elias, that is, not the herald: indicating power; but I show the humility at which you take offense: as if he said: Serve the humble one before the exalted one judges. Behold, I am neither the Christ, nor a judge on the side of power.
1.23: 1.23 I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness. He does not say, I am a man, or John, or the son of Zachary. He does not consider human subsistence or generation, but the forerunner of the Word, exalted beyond all these things, leaves behind everything contained within the world. He ascends on high, made the voice of the Word; he confesses no substance in himself except the abundance of grace by which he surpasses every creature, so as to be the voice of the Word. The voice is the interpreter of the mind, and the mind, that is, the intellect of all, is the Son of God. John, therefore, is the voice and interpreter of this mind, because he first showed him to the world: Behold the Lamb of God. Isaias prophesied this of John: I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, in which the word sounds, that is, prophecy, and the showing and the lamp of the present word.
1.24: 1.24 They were of the Pharisees. That is, of the princes of the Jews, who do not seek doctrine, but envy. Yet they come to John for this reason, because they hear that he preached the common resurrection of all, which they themselves also believed; hence they agree with Christ in many things. They also heard the apostle Paul in many things.
1.25: 1.25 Why then dost thou baptize? The Pharisees heard in the prophets that Christ would come and baptize, knowing that the Jordan bore a figure of baptism, and that Elias and Eliseus crossed it with dry feet, and they did not doubt that the figure of baptism had preceded in Elias and Eliseus, hence they now thought that they had risen again and were baptizing; hence they do not ask, Art thou one of the prophets? but only: Art thou the prophet? that is, the one who prefigured baptism.
1.26: 1.26 I baptize with water. Let not what I do be imputed to audacity, because I wash bodies with water, I do not take away sins, so that as I am the forerunner by being born and preaching, so also by baptizing; but he who takes away sins is in the midst of you.
1.27: 1.27 The latchet of whose shoe I am not worthy, etc. He does not say I will not loose. For he did loose, since he made him manifest and opened many things about his divinity and humanity; but, I am not worthy, because he reckons himself unworthy to do this, in which humility is simply indicated.
1.28: 1.28 These things were done in Bethania. There are two Bethanias. One beyond the Jordan, the other near, not far from Jerusalem, where Lazarus was raised up. The one that is beyond the Jordan signifies human nature under the natural law before the streams of grace, which grace was abundant after the incarnation of Christ; which nature was created for this, to obey the law of nature, in which John baptizes, because it does not free from sin. He baptizes beyond the streams of divine gifts, which had not yet begun in Christ to descend upon human nature. The one that is this side of the Jordan signifies the same human nature obedient under the law of grace, which is nearest to Jerusalem, that is, to the vision of peace, through charity, in which Christ raises the dead because he frees from sin.
1.29: 1.29 The next day John saw Jesus. Typically. John, that is the people of grace, on the next day, that is, after the law, recognizes the lamb by whom it is redeemed. Coming to him, and he saith. Not only with steps of the body, but also with the approaches of his interior contemplation, because he deigned to be known by John according to divinity and humanity. Behold the Lamb of God, etc. The lamb furnishes three things to those who possess it: milk of simple doctrine, by which little ones are nourished; wool, that is, increases of virtues; the eating of his flesh. The sin of the world. The sin of the world is called original sin, which is common to the whole world, in which the whole human nature, created together and at once, transgressed the divine laws through disobedience in paradise; this original sin, and each sin added to it, grace remits.
1.30: 1.30 After me cometh a man. Christ is man, in which he is fitting for us and pays for us, and Son of God, in which he is fitting for the Father and, by forgiving sins, reconciles us to him.
1.31: 1.31 That he may be made manifest. This is the lamb who takes away sins, which I do not, whom I also now know better, but I baptize for this reason, that he may be made manifest to Israel. For lest, on account of arrogance, they should be less baptized by Christ in the Spirit, he prepared the way for him by the practice of baptizing; hence after one has come to him, who is the way, his baptism ceases. In the baptism of John also the humility of Christ is made manifest, which is the fulfillment of all justice; for as it was needful for Christ to be born and to die, so also to be baptized. For if he who has no need is baptized by a servant, let not even the wise and holy, however great, disdain to be baptized by the Lord, without whom they remain in sins. Baptizing. Christ is baptized by John, to indicate all humility, which is all justice. But not alone, lest the baptism of John, in which God made man was baptized, should seem holier and greater than the baptism of Christ, in which men are baptized. Others, however, are baptized by John, that the practice of baptizing may prepare the way for the baptism of Christ.
1.32: 1.32 And testimony. As he said that he came to make Christ manifest, so he bore testimony, namely he saw the spirit. In this he learned what he previously did not know: he had come also to preach penance, that is, to make the preparation for the preaching of Christ, but he sets down singularly only about the preparation of baptism, because the baptism of Christ is the highest sacrament among the others. The Spirit descending. Not that he then descended for the first time, but that by this descending it may be shown that he remains in those baptized with water and not otherwise, and that John through him might understand Christ more excellently.
1.33: 1.33 And I knew him not. AUG. Having seen the dove, he says that through it he learned what he did not know before, etc., up to hence the Apostle: They differ in labor and mind, but are not different in operation. HIER. He shows that John did not know through the baptism of Christ, that is, that the world was redeemed, for he knew that he was the Son of God, and born in the flesh. Aug. says that John was ignorant only of this, whether he would keep for himself the power of baptizing or assign it to one of his own. And remaining. AUG. Spiritually the spirit is said to remain in Christ, from whom he never departed through sin, in whom he always wonderfully lived and wonderfully worked; he comes upon the saints, and departs through sins. Yet he always remains in them for something, as Christ promised them, namely that they may always persevere in good things. For something he does not remain, namely that they prophesy by him, or work miracles, and therefore what he says is the first sign for recognizing Christ. He that baptizeth. Christ baptizes in the spirit, not only by remitting sins in water, but also afterwards by purging, and kindling love, and filling with gifts. This is the Son of God. Here he testifies to the Son of God whom above he called man: that from him testimony of both natures may be had.
1.35: 1.35 The next day again John stood. Typically. John stands, the law ceases, yet bearing testimony to Christ. Jesus walks, that is, grace gathering from here and there.
1.37: 1.37 They followed Jesus. They followed in order to hear him now rather than John, yet not as yet adhering to him entirely, but to see where he dwells, that they may come to him constantly and be instructed by him, and afterwards they followed perfectly, when he called them from the boat. Two follow, because those who follow ought to be kindled with a twofold charity.
1.38: 1.38 Turning. They had seen him as it were from behind, but he as it were offered his face to them when he descended from majesty so that he could be seen, when in place of the shadow of the law he displayed the light of the Gospel. What seek you? He asks not in ignorance, but that those who answer may have a reward, who answer the thing, not the person, what, not whom, lest he seem to show himself; they answer him with the person. Where dwellest thou? Mystically. They want to be shown in whom Christ dwells, that they may make themselves like them. Or, those who see the incarnation devoutly seek to be shown how the eternal dwelling is with the Father.
1.39: 1.39 Come. As if it cannot be explained in speech, but is shown by deed: come by believing and working, and you will understand; come by the testimony of John and depart from the law, and you will receive grace. That day. It shows the New Testament, or the present life. And it was about the tenth hour. Because they had come from the law, the decalogue sent them to Christ; at the tenth hour they seek to be taught by him, because none other teaches the law than he who gave it. He teaches, however, with mercy, and those things are fulfilled which they could not fulfill; or the tenth hour indicates the evening of the world.
1.40: 1.40 Brother of Simon Peter, one of the two who had heard of John, and followed him. The younger brother believes first, for the order of faith is not empty. Perhaps Andrew is called the brother of Peter for dignity, upon whom, that is upon whose faith, the Church was to be founded.
1.41: 1.41 He findeth first. True piety at once announces the treasure found to a brother, that as he is a brother in blood, he may also be a brother in faith. We have found the Messias, etc. Christ in Greek, Messias in Hebrew, anointed in Latin, for he was truly anointed by the Holy Spirit in a special way, from which anointing Christians are named. That Jacob set up a stone after the vision as a pillar which the pouring of oil anointed, he already understood divinely through that rock the future rock, namely Christ, to be anointed with the Holy Spirit, figuratively, on which rock he prefigured the Church being founded, etc.
1.42: 1.42 Thou art Simon the son. First he says the name as he has it from his parents, so that the change may be signified, when he calls Peter from Simon. In the change, however, the liveliness of the mystery is noted, but even the former name lacks not power. For Simon is the obedient son of grace or of a dove, when he comes to Jesus, following his brother; hence from the rock Christ he is called Peter, weak in him, in figure of the Church which is founded on the rock. Thou art Simon. CHRYS. He changed the name to show that it is he who gave the Old Testament and changed names, for he called Abram Abraham, and Sarai Sara, and Jacob Israel. Names, then, he imposed on many even from birth, as on Isaac and Samson, but on others after the name given by their parents, as on Peter and the sons of Zebedee. For those whose virtue was to shine from an early age received names from then; those whose virtue was to be increased afterwards had the naming placed afterwards. Son of Jona, etc. Jona and Joanna are used indifferently. Jona is interpreted dove, Joanna grace.
1.43: 1.43 Into Galilee, and he findeth Philip. Galilee means transmigration, or revelation. For man passes over from vices to virtues, and then from virtue to virtue, and thus revelation is made to him, so that the God of gods is seen in Sion. About to call a disciple to follow, that is, to imitate, he goes out into Galilee, hinting by the very place that as he himself advanced in wisdom, and as through sufferings he entered into glory, so also his followers.
1.44: 1.44 From Bethsaida, the city. The city is not named in vain, nor is it called that of Philip, Peter and Andrew in vain. For it means house of hunters, in which the mind and office of these men is noted: for they are hunters in catching souls, hence Philip, before he becomes an apostle, of his own accord calls Nathanael.
1.45: 1.45 Philip findeth, etc. Nathanael, most skilled in the Scriptures, understands what others do not, namely that the singular Nazarene comes out of Nazareth: but because he was most learned, he was not chosen as an apostle: for all the apostles were first taken from the unlearned, that the wise may be confounded. Of whom Moses wrote. As a wary hunter, he establishes the truth to his brother by many reasons, namely that Jesus is the one foretold in the law and the prophets. The son of Joseph, who is of the house of David, so that through him (not that he was born of him) together with Mary his mother (who he knew from the prophets would bear as a virgin) he may be marked as being of David.
1.46: 1.46 And Nathanael said to him. Either he asks doubting, or he affirms as one skilled in the law, that from a city of so great a name there can be some good man, or an eminent teacher, or the supreme Savior. For Nazareth means flower, or shoot of cleanness, or holiness. To both ways of pronouncing it, the following is fittingly added: Come and see, etc.
1.47: 1.47 Behold an Israelite indeed. Guile, that is, pretense. For if he has sins, he confesses them. He does not therefore deny that he is a sinner, but in him he praises confession. The Pharisees, however, are guileful, who proclaim themselves good while they are evil.
1.48: 1.48 Whence knowest thou me? Recognizing that the Lord is speaking of his conscience, he asks not from indignation but with wonder, whence and by what power. Under the fig tree I saw thee. AUG. Nathanael, that is, gift of God, is the true people of Israel, gift of God, who was hidden under the fig tree, that is, subject under the habit of sinning and the shadow of death, as the first parents covered themselves under the leaves of the fig; where he had first been seen and sought by the Lord before he saw and sought the Lord, and even before he called him through the apostles.
1.49: 1.49 Rabbi, thou art the Son of God. Because Nathanael recognized that Christ, though absent, had seen what he himself had done in another place, that is, how and where he was called by Philip, which is a mark of Deity, he confesses him not only master but also Son of God, and king of Israel, that is, Christ, in whom he is proved to be an Israelite, as is said, that is, seeing God.
1.51: 1.51 You shall see heaven open. Nathanael the Israelite is said to be about to see heaven open, and the angels of God descending and ascending, as once the patriarch Jacob saw a ladder and angels ascending and descending, who by a blessing was called Israel. The angels of God. This miracle often appeared, that angels ascended and descended upon Christ. Upon the Son of man. Christ says he is the Son of man, affirming what is less, namely humanity, Nathanael and Peter the Son of God, which is greater, affirming divinity. Behold the confirmation of both natures in Christ. These confessing the deity deserve to ascend; he asserting humanity testifies that he came to redeem. Upon the Son of man. He confirms that he is man lest some err, believing him to be only God, as even Peter when he said: Be it far from thee, Lord.
2.1: 2.1 And the third day. AUG. After the manifestation of Christ through the testimonies of John, he showed himself by a miracle. And the day. The third day signifies, that is, the time of grace, after the time, that is, before the law and under the law, that Christ came through the flesh to the wedding of the Church.
2.2: 2.2 And Jesus also was invited. In which he shows that the wedding he made is not to be despised, and he suggests the sacrament of marriage.
2.3: 2.3 Wanting. The wine fails, so that, the wine being wonderfully made from water, the power of the hidden Deity may appear. AUG. Greater power is in the creation and governance of heaven and earth, etc., up to through which the power that works also in greater things is brought back to memory.
2.4: 2.4 What is there between me and thee. THE SAME. In these words he does not deny his mother, as the heretics say, etc., up to understands the entrance to God, drinks wine.
2.6: 2.6 Two or. THE SAME. It is the way of one reckoning to say this, so as to say two for what are also three, etc., up to scattered among the three sons of Noe.
2.7: 2.7 And they filled. That the water-pots were filled at his command signifies that even that Scripture is from the Lord, but while Christ lies hidden in it under a veil, that is, under the covering of the letter, it tastes like insipid water. But when the veil is taken away, it is intoxicating wine. He who creates all things from nothing could indeed have filled them empty with wine, but he preferred to make wine from water, to teach that he does not dissolve the law but fulfills it, nor in the Gospel does or teaches other things than what prophecy foretold.
2.9: 2.9 And when he had tasted. The triclinium, that is three orders of those reclining, differing from each other in height, that is, teachers, the continent, the married. The architriclinus is some man skilled in the law, who drinks the spiritual sense of the law. Hence to open the spiritual sense in the Scriptures to the disciples is to turn water into wine, as when after the resurrection he opened their sense that they might understand the Scriptures. The water made wine. By water, the baptism of John; by wine, the passion of Christ; hence the wine is first brought to the architriclinus, that is, to John, who drank the passion before Christ.
2.11: 2.11 This beginning did Jesus. HIER. At the beginning of the signs which, mortal, he was going to give to mortals, he turned water into wine, as, now immortal, he opened to the disciples the sense, so that they might understand Christ in the law and the prophets; so he first imbued carnal minds with the taste of wisdom, about to fulfill them afterwards, raised up, with greater glory.
2.12: 2.12 After this, etc. After the beginning of the signs about the wine, he adds another indication of divine majesty in the casting out of the sellers from the temple. Typically. The Son of God, as humble, goes down to Capharnaum, that is into the world, according as he has a mother and brethren.
2.13: 2.13 And the Pasch was at hand. We keep the Pasch when we pass from vices to virtues. For this Jesus comes when he visits the Church daily and considers each one's acts, and casts out those who among the saints do good things in pretense, or openly do evil. By the oxen that plow are signified the preachers of heavenly doctrine; these they sell who preach not out of love of God, but for temporal gain. The innocent sheep furnish their fleeces for clothing; by these are signified works of cleanness and piety, which are sold when they are done for human praise. The Spirit appeared as a dove, hence by the dove the spirit is understood, which the Simoniacs sell. They give money on loan in the Church who serve not feignedly heavenly things but openly earthly things. All these are cast out of the part of the lot of the saints, who do good things in pretense or evil openly, and are now scourged with the cords of sins for correction; who, if they remain uncorrected, will be bound at the end. He casts out the sheep and oxen also, because he shows the life and doctrine of such to be reprobate. And he overthrew the tables, because in the end the very things they loved are destroyed. And he went up. If he himself who gave the decrees of God keeps them, he teaches how great care men should have to be free for prayers and the solemnities of God. We read that he went up twice to the Pasch. Once in the first year of preaching, John not yet imprisoned, which is what is treated here. Second, when he went to his passion; and in both he cast the sellers out of the temple.
2.14: 2.14 And he found in the temple. If in the figurative temple, which is a house of prayer, he forbids trading, which is thought honest since it concerns things offered in the temple, how much more does he forbid drinking bouts and other graver things?
2.15: 2.15 Of cords. The cords with which they are cast out are the increases of evil actions, hence Isaias: Woe to you that draw iniquity with cords of vanity Isa. 5.. And Solomon: Every one is held with the cords of his own sins Prov. 5..
2.16: 2.16 To them that sold doves. Not only those selling doves, but others also make the house of God a house of traffic, that is all who seek the things that are their own, not the things that are Jesus Christ's.
2.17: 2.17 The zeal of thy house. AUG. Good zeal is a fervor of mind by which the mind, casting aside human fear, is kindled for the defense of truth. He is eaten up by it who strives to correct any wrong he sees; if he cannot, he tolerates and groans.
2.18: 2.18 What sign dost thou show unto us, seeing thou dost these things? He answered. Because they ask a sign why he casts the usual commerce out of the temple? and he says: Destroy. As if he said: Because this temple signifies the temple of the body in which there is no stain, and deservedly I purge this figurative one, I who am able by divine power to raise that one up when destroyed by men through death.
2.20: 2.20 The Jews then said. The carnal tasted carnally, he spoke spiritually. This the Evangelist opens to us: But he spoke of the temple of his body. Forty-six. AUG. Anatole in Greek is east, dysis west, arctos north, etc., up to which contain the number six forty-six times. Was built. AUG. The building of Solomon was completed in seven years, etc., up to hence it is said that the elect are to be gathered from the four winds.
2.23: 2.23 Now when. He attended the gatherings, to convert more by words and signs. And because some, moved by signs alone, believed in him, truly indeed, but yet in such a way that they could afterwards be scandalized at his passion, and because they were not yet born again of water and the spirit, they were not worthy for Jesus to trust himself to them and dwell familiarly with them. For he knew what was in them, better than man himself of himself. This faith suits the catechumens, who believe in him, but because they are not born again, the communion of the body and blood of Christ is not entrusted to them. Of such was Nicodemus, who believing says that he came from God, on account of the signs he had seen, but he was not yet born again, and therefore came by night, not by day, because not yet enlightened by heavenly light.
3.1: 3.1 Now there was a man, etc. This was one of those who had believed through signs. Nicodemus by name. Nicodemus, victory of the people, or victor of the people, bearing the figure of all who from the Jewish people, believing in Christ, overcome the world by faith.
3.2: 3.2 The same came, etc. Night signifies the letter of the law, or ignorance of heart, or fear. And perhaps he came by night because, a master in Israel, he would be ashamed to speak openly, or for fear of the Jews. Because he prudently noted the open signs, he more fully seeks the mysteries of faith, and therefore deserved to be taught about the deity of Christ and both his births, about the passion, resurrection and ascension, about the second generation, and the entrance into the kingdom of heaven, and many other things.
3.3: 3.3 Amen, amen I say. He does not explain the second birth to one who asks, lest Nicodemus believe that faith alone, for which he had believed in Jesus on seeing the signs, suffices for salvation without the power of spiritual regeneration, and without the sacraments. Also because Nicodemus understood him as a mere man like John the Baptist or any of the prophets, Jesus therefore began to instruct him about the second regeneration, by which he understands him to be the Son of God, and himself able to become a son of God. AUG. The second birth about which Jesus teaches is spiritual, which is of God and the Church unto life, but he tastes only the carnal, which is of Adam and Eve unto death. But as this man says the carnal cannot be repeated, so also the spiritual, by whomever performed, cannot be repeated. For they are born of the seed of the true Abraham, whether through the free woman or through the bondwoman. Unless a man. The visible sacrament of water is necessary for the washing of the visible body, as the doctrine of invisible faith is necessary, and for the sanctification of the invisible soul. Be born again. CHRYS. That is, if you are not born from above, and do not receive certainty of doctrines somewhere else, you err outside and are far from the kingdom of heaven, showing and indicating himself here, since it is not only this that is seen, but other eyes are needed to see God.
3.5: 3.5 Of water. Of water, the visible sacrament, and the spirit, invisible in understanding, that he may receive the symbol of baptism visibly, and complete the spiritual understanding of the symbol itself. Or of visible water and the Holy Spirit.
3.6: 3.6 That which is born. He distinguishes this spiritual birth from the carnal, saying: That which is born. Of the flesh. That is, of the first man by succession of flesh, is carnal. By the name of flesh he signifies not only the flesh, but the whole carnal man. So, on the contrary, the whole spiritual man, in soul and body, is called spirit. And that, etc. By word and sacrament the spirit is invisibly present, by whom one born of Adam is born unto death, a Son of God unto life, who is called not only spiritual but spirit, because as the substance of spirit is invisible, so invisibly through a visible sacrament he is made a Son of God. Is spirit. Do not wonder if I call one so born spirit, because as the spirit breatheth where he will, and thou knowest not whence he cometh or whither he goeth, so is every one that is born of the spirit.
3.8: 3.8 The Spirit breatheth where he will. Which he has in his power, whose heart he may enlighten. You hear his voice in the Scriptures, or when someone full of the Holy Spirit speaks, and though you hear it, you know not whence it comes, that is, how it entered his heart or how it returned, because his nature is invisible. So is every one that is born of the Holy Spirit, because by the Spirit working invisibly he begins to be what he was not, so that the unbeliever knows not whence he comes and whither he goes, that is, by what grace he came into the adoption of the Son, and goes into the kingdom of God. Since these things are unknown to the carnal man, he asks again? How can these things be done, not having a spiritual understanding in the letter of the law; he thinks impossible what is said of birth through the spirit, hence he is rebuked by the Lord: Thou art a master, etc. And his voice, etc. The voice of the spirit is the voice of Christ, which Nicodemus heard, but because he is not yet born of the spirit, he knows not whence it cometh or whither it goeth, that is, on what occasion he wills man to be born in the spirit, or whither it goes, that is, to what perfection he says the one born of him comes. For he who is born of him is made one spirit with him by grace, as he himself also is one spirit by nature.
3.10: 3.10 Thou art a master, etc. He does not insult him, as being held superior to him who is over all, but because he wants him to be born of the spirit, which none can be unless humble, he humbles the puffed-up man by his mastership. As if he said: Proud prince, you know nothing; be humbled like him who emptied himself and was born of the spirit, and you will know what you now know not.
3.11: 3.11 We speak what we know. That is, because he himself is the knowledge, the speech and the word of the Father. And we testify what we have seen. Because he himself is the vision, and the true testimony and truth of the Father. The plural hints at the mystery of the Trinity.
3.12: 3.12 If I have spoken to you earthly things. AUG. And since you do not receive earthly things, how can you grasp heavenly things, that is, the heavenly birth of the spirit? since you not only do not believe, but do not even understand earthly things, such as what I said about the temple of my body (which I took from the earth), to be destroyed by you, raised up by me.
3.13: 3.13 But he that descended. This pertains to the second birth in the spirit, because no one ascends to the Father in Christ unless he is born of the spirit. No one is saved by the death of Christ unless he is born of the spirit. No one is born of the spirit except in the death of Christ. And when he says Son of man, he gives us certainty of ascending, since we are sons of men.
3.14: 3.14 And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert. He adds about his own death, which is the origin and cause of having the aforesaid things, in the faith of which he instructs him. And because he was carnal, and known in the law, he therefore brings forward a certain part of the law, which he shows to be a figure and significative of his death, so that thus it may also be clear about the other parts of the law that they are in figure. And because death is understood by the serpent, and Christ dead is called a serpent, whom he who looks at him in faith is freed, as by looking at that one in figure they are freed from the fiery serpents, which signify the incentives of vices. So must the Son of man be lifted up, etc. He invites the master of the law to the signification of the law. And because he had spoken of the Son of man, lest Nicodemus think this only, he adds that the same is also the Son of God. For so God loved. He opens the cause of human salvation, namely the love of God the Father, from whom all restoration is through his Son in the Holy Spirit.
3.16: 3.16 The world. Cosmos in Greek, which in Latin is translated mundus, means adornment. By 'world', therefore, human nature is signified, not because it consists of the four elements according to the body, but because according to the soul it has been adorned by God and made to the image of God, and for this reason God loves it, so as to make it eternal. That he might give his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth, etc. Behold, he says the same of the Son of God as he said above of the Son of man, so that through him by whom we were created in the Godhead, through the same we may be restored in the man.
3.19: 3.19 And this is the judgment. Why is the one who does not believe judged? Because the light has come which rouses men and admonishes them to recognize their own evils, in which all are, but some hate the light that admonishes, and flee, lest their evils, which they love, be exposed. Others, admonished by the light, accuse their own evils, which is to do the truth, and so they are enlightened. For they were their own. He who is in darkness and loves the light is not evil, but he is called evil, and his works evil, who after the light has come hates the light and loves evil things. And this is what he says: For their works were evil. Works, that is, impiety, and unbelief, and hatred of the eternal light, and the refusal to look upon it, but the wish to remain in the darkness of sins.
3.21: 3.21 But he that doth. Having shown by what justice the one who does not believe is condemned, he shows by what justice the one who believes is saved. But he that doth. That is, he to whom his own evils are displeasing and who accuses them, does not pardon himself, does not spare himself, but comes to the light. And he begins to act together with God who accuses evils, because the beginning of good is the accusation of evil; therefore his works, namely this, that he accuses himself as God accuses, are made manifest, because they are done in God; for unless the light of God shone for him, he would not be displeased with himself.
3.22: 3.22 After these things. Not immediately after the discussion with Nicodemus, which took place in Jerusalem, but after a space of time had passed he returned from Galilee into Judea. Into the land of Judea, and there he abode, etc. Morally: where there is confession of sins or of divine praises, there Jesus comes, and his disciples, that is, his teaching and enlightenment, where he abides purging from transgressions; hence follows, and there he abode and baptized. And John also was baptizing. While Christ was already baptizing, John still baptizes, because the shadow still remains. Nor ought the forerunner to cease until the truth is made manifest.
3.24: 3.24 For John was not yet cast into prison. Behold, he clearly notes the deeds of Christ before John's imprisonment, which the others passed over, beginning from those things which were done after John was cast into prison, when, the baptism of the forerunner ceasing, the baptism of Christ openly began.
3.25: 3.25 And there arose a question between some of John's disciples, etc. While John preaches, and his school endures, Christ preaches and works in secret, but baptizes openly, so that a question may arise about the baptism of John and the baptism of Christ, and that it may be resolved by the testimonies of John.
3.26: 3.26 And they came to John and said to him: Rabbi, etc. Wishing to accuse Christ, whom a little before they had seen baptized by John.
3.27: 3.27 John answered and said, etc. Because I was born, beyond the custom of human nature, of parents advanced in age, you think me to be above men. But know that I am a mere man, he is God, from whom I have whatever I have. From myself is weakness, from him the loftiness of grace. Do you think I would say anything against my own testimony? I do not baptize unto the remission of sins, but he does. A man cannot. As if to say: I, a mere man, have nothing except what has been given by God, that is, to baptize unto repentance, not unto remission, because I am not the Christ, but he is, as you know that I have testified to you; therefore run to him.
3.28: 3.28 I am not the Christ. I am not anointed by the Father with the fullness of the Spirit, but I have received from his fullness, so as to go before him.
3.29: 3.29 This my joy therefore. In this my joy is full, that I have become the friend of the bridegroom, and that I stand and rejoice.
3.30: 3.30 He must increase. I rejoice at the voice of the bridegroom. The bridegroom will increase, that is, he will be found to be the Christ, who was thought to be a prophet. I shall decrease, because I shall be found to be his prophet, who was thought to be the Christ. He must increase. That is, be exalted, that is, while he forgives sins he gives grace, in which his glory, which is always perfect in itself, increases in man, while man sees and possesses it more. Man is diminished who before glorified in himself, as long as he confesses his sins and receives what he gives. To this the passion of both bears witness: Christ is exalted on the cross, John is diminished by the head. The creation also bears witness. John was born when the days were decreasing, Christ when they were increasing.
3.31: 3.31 But I must decrease. John is a figure of the law; Christ is the truth; the law is diminished when the truth appears. He that cometh from above is above all, etc. ALC. That is, from the height of human nature before the sin of the first parent, etc., up to secondly according to the height of the Father, to whom he is equal. Of the earth. That is, he who is born of earthly parents, from whom he has contracted sin and the punishment of sin, is nothing of himself except earth. And what he hath seen. Since he himself is the Son of God, the Word of the Father, he does not hear some other word of the Father, nor testify it to men, but he knows and makes known to men that he himself is the Word which the Father spoke, that is, brought forth and begot from himself, and that he is from the Father. The Evangelist says this as he was able, what cannot be fully said or understood.
3.33: 3.33 Hath set his seal that God. That is, he has placed a sign in his heart, as something special, namely that this is the true God, who has been sent for the salvation of men. Is true. For he whom God hath sent. Every man of himself is a liar; for he cannot speak true things unless enlightened by God. For he whom God the Father has sent speaks the words of God; what does this mean? He whom God has sent is God; therefore he speaks the words of God; therefore the words of the Son, bearing witness of himself that he is God, are the words of God. He speaketh the words of God. In this he distinguishes himself from Christ, but because he is sent and speaks the words of God, he adds more openly: For God doth not give the Spirit by measure. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand. To men he gives by measure; to the Son he does not give by measure, but just as he begot his Son, whole from himself whole, so to his incarnate Son he gave his whole Spirit, not in part, not by subdivisions, but generally and universally, and he gives for no other reason than that the Father loves the Son.
3.36: 3.36 He that believeth in the Son hath life everlasting; but he that, etc. As if he were to say: he who believes in the Son has the Son himself, and through this has life. But the wrath of God abideth on him. The wrath with which he was born remains, and therefore he does not say 'comes' but 'abides', because through the Son sent, who is life, the effect of that wrath, namely death, corruption, etc., is not removed; all of which remain.
4.1: 4.1 When Jesus therefore understood. Jesus knew their knowledge and envy, that they had not learned about him in order to follow him, but to persecute him, and therefore he fled, teaching his own to yield to evils, not out of fear, nor as unable to escape them. And baptizeth. Which is truly said, for he himself always cleanses in the Spirit invisibly and by gift, but his baptism also takes place in the body, which is in two things, namely in water and the word of life; hence Paul: Cleansing it by the laver of water in the word of life. Eph. 5.
4.2: 4.2 Though Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples. In whose baptism the Spirit was given, though not so manifestly as after the Ascension he was given in an ineffable and unthinkable manner.
4.3: 4.3 He left Judea. That is, the unbelieving Pharisees, who were planning to persecute him on account of his baptism, which was growing, and because they understood that through his teaching the law was being made void. And went. After he had received a few of the Jewish people, he left the unbelievers who followed the letter of the law, which leads no one to perfection. And he went into Galilee, that is, into the spiritual understanding of that very letter. Into Galilee. In Galilee the transfiguration of the Lord is believed to have taken place, by which is signified the transformation of human nature into its former glory. In Galilee he gave his disciples, on the mountain, the teaching by which believers are to pass over to life.
4.4: 4.4 He must needs. Between Judea and Galilee lies Samaria, that is, between the law of the letter, which is through Judea, and the divine laws revolving around God, of which Galilee is the figure, there is the natural law established in the middle; since, therefore, he took the foundations of the Church from the law, it was necessary for him to cross to the Gentiles established under the law of nature, so that with both he might return to the Galilee of eternal blessedness.
4.5: 4.5 He cometh therefore. So that the Samaritans, who claimed for themselves the inheritance of the patriarch Israel, might recognize him and be converted to him. Which is called Sichar. Sichar, that is, conclusion, or branch, that is, the Gentile people shut up under sin, who are a branch cut from the wild olive and grafted into the olive.
4.6: 4.6 Now there was, etc. Because natural reason arises from no other source than from the cause of all good things, it is fittingly called the fountain of Jacob, that is, reason proceeding from the infinite height of the Father. Jesus therefore, being wearied, etc. Allegorically: the journey of Jesus is the assumption of flesh, in which there is weariness, that is, weakness, relieving man whom he created by power; his sitting is humility. The sixth hour is the sixth age in which he came; the well is the depth of this world. The Samaritan woman is the Church, who comes not yet just but to be justified. The water of the well is the desire of this world, which is drawn as from the deep, men being bent and inclined toward it, with cupidity sent before like a water-pot. He sat. As relieving his weariness, wherein the master is shown as about to teach and to possess those who approach. Above. A fountain is so called wherever water flows from the earth, but if only on the surface it is a fountain, if in the depth it is also called a well.
4.7: 4.7 There cometh. In figure of the Church from the Gentiles, which formerly drew water, that is, pleasure, from the depth of the world, whose faith Jesus thirsts for and asks to be given drink by her. GREG. Or the woman, that is, the Synagogue, who comes to draw water, etc., up to the primitive Church. Give me. Jesus, sitting upon the fountain, asks from the primitive Church, which he had chosen from the Gentiles, the drink of faith, by which he is believed in; he asks from nature the drink of reason, by which the creator and redeemer is investigated. The apostles sent into the city, that is, into the world, to buy spiritual food, that is, faith, and action, and knowledge, with which the masters of the Church are satisfied. Give me. Although Jesus, after weariness, could thirst, yet he does not demand this drink, but desires that the heart of the Church of the Gentiles, through knowledge of his labor, may become a drink to him.
4.8: 4.8 For his disciples. The disciples had gone into the city, namely to the Jews, who were fortified by the valley of the law and armed with the weapons of prophecy, to buy their food, namely, preparing hearts for God by the preaching of the faith.
4.9: 4.9 Then that Samaritan woman saith to him. Not knowing what drink he asks of her, thinking it to be about water, she objects that she is of foreign vessels, whose company the Jews do not even use; but Jesus, who was asking for faith, desired to give her the Spirit, and he admonishes her to ask; and the Spirit is both the gift of God and living water. For the Jews, etc. The Jews detest the Samaritans and call them supplanters, because they deprived them of the inheritance of their father Jacob, by abstaining from their foods and vessels.
4.10: 4.10 Jesus answered. Step by step and with simple words he instructs her, so that at last she may be able to receive the gift of God, that is, the Spirit.
4.11: 4.11 The woman saith to him. Living water is called only that which is received where it springs up; of which the woman, carnally wise, said: Thou hast nothing to draw with, and the well is deep; whence then hast thou living water? But lest he should seem perhaps to promise another fountain, she adds: Art thou greater, that is, canst thou be better, than our father Jacob, who used this well with his own? Against which Christ openly shows that he speaks not carnally but spiritually, saying that he who drinks of his water shall not thirst.
4.12: 4.12 Art thou greater. The foreigner calls Jacob her father, because she had lived under the law of Moses and possessed the land which Jacob had given to his son. AUG. The water-pot is cupidity, the water pleasure; it is replenished, not quenched. And himself drank thereof. From the well men and cattle drink, and likewise from reason, as it were depraved and obscured, it is dug and worked with great labor; and some drink as men, who use that reason for good, like the saints. Others as cattle, who use it for evil, like the philosophers.
4.13: 4.13 But whosoever. Whoever shall have lent his heart to my preaching and shall have known the gift of grace, the faith which worketh by charity is born in him, and thus at last he will pass into eternal life.
4.14: 4.14 Water. Bodily water flows downward; spiritual water springs upward and carries with it those who drink it into eternal glory.
4.16: 4.16 Go, call thy husband, etc. That under his leading you may ascend to the contemplation of spiritual understanding: go, call thy husband. You, the sensual part, call the rational intellect, by which you may be ruled as by a husband, you who now are wise carnally; I, the light and head of the husband, will enlighten him. As if to say: These things which I say are to be understood not carnally, as you, being animal, do, but spiritually, and are to be received under the guidance of reason, and therefore prepare the understanding for me and come, understanding these spiritual things which I say.
4.17: 4.17 The woman answered. In truth this woman then had no husband, but was using one who was not lawful, about whom she answers still carnally wise, not having yet called her husband, that is, understanding. Jesus saith to her. Gradually raising her, he still speaks mysteries, so as gradually to lead her to know who it was that spoke with her. And not a good work: he does not praise the woman's answer as prudent, but praises the confession of the truth.
4.18: 4.18 For thou hast had five husbands. The five husbands are the five laws given to human nature. The first, in paradise before sin, in the prohibition of the tree. The second, after the transgression and expulsion from paradise, concerning the multiplication of the human race. The third, to Noe before the flood, about building the ark. The fourth, after the flood, about the divisions of the nations. The fifth, to Abraham, about circumcision and the sacrifice of his son. To these five laws, as to five husbands, the human soul was subject from the beginning of the world until Moses; afterward the law of the letter was given, which conferred no salvation, whence it is said: He whom thou now hast is not thy husband. Leave the letter, go to the spirit of the letter, to the New Testament, from which you may conceive the spiritual offspring of virtues. AUG. Five husbands, that is, the five senses of the body, have ruled you; now in the time of discernment, no husband rules you, that is, the understanding of wisdom, but an adulterer, that is, error corrupts, while you take carnally what I say; and therefore call your husband, so that (as I say) you may understand spiritually. The five senses are called husbands in the younger age because they are lawful. For after the fall of man and by the decree of God that age is naturally governed, not toward eternal things, but toward these temporal things, to be desired if they soothe, to be avoided if they offend.
4.19: 4.19 Sir, I perceive that thou art a prophet. The woman, advancing from what she had heard, had already begun in some measure to have understanding, whence she calls him a prophet, but not fully, because she does not believe that Christ has come.
4.20: 4.20 Our fathers, etc. You are a prophet, and therefore judge concerning this contention which moves me. The Jews preferred themselves to the Samaritans on account of the temple which Solomon built, in which they worshipped. On the other hand the Samaritans were against the Jews on account of the mountain, on which and not in the temple the fathers worshipped who pleased God. And so the patriarchs worshipped on mountains, the Jews in the temple, prefiguring the manner of praying well.
4.21: 4.21 Woman. In this place the Lord represses the boasting of the Samaritans, who thought themselves of no less religion than the Jews. He speaks, therefore, in the person of the prophets and of all who believe in Christ; hence he says: You adore that which you know not, because no one adores the Father unless he adores the Son, through whom one comes to the knowledge of the Father, but we know the Son, and through the Son the Father, whence follows: For salvation is of the Jews, etc., that is, because Christ, who is salvation, is of the Jews, not only by origin of the flesh, but also faith and the primitive Church arose from them. Believe me. Because there is now in you a husband who can believe, and therefore believe: for unless you believe, you shall not understand. Isa. 7. When neither on this mountain. Behold, equally your mountain and the temple of the Jews will be reprobated, but in this you are unequal, that you Samaritans adore what you know not, but we Jews, not all, but the elect, adore what we know, because the knowledge of God is a testament to us; prophecy was promised; Christ is from us, and this is why salvation is of the Jews; but although we are thus different, nevertheless I do not prefer the place of the Jews to the place of the Samaritans, and this is it.
4.23: 4.23 But the hour cometh, and now is, when. Before I came in the flesh, no one could adore the Father in spirit and in truth, except the patriarchs and prophets, to whom my incarnation was revealed, but through my presence in the flesh true adorers shall be made. In spirit and in truth. Not in the temple, not on this mountain, but inwardly, in the innermost temple of the heart and in the truth of knowledge, the Father is to be adored.
4.24: 4.24 God is a spirit. Since God is spirit and not body, he does not seek a bodily place, a mountain or temple, in which he may be prayed to, but a pure spirit is his temple, in which he is prayed to, not concerning visible things which pass away, but concerning eternal things which are the truth.
4.25: 4.25 I know that the Messias cometh, who is called, etc. Now, advanced further by the words of the one teaching, she knows by whom she ought to be perfectly instructed, that is, by the Messias. When he is come, he will tell us all things. Jesus saith to her. How, despising temple and mountain, we should adore in spirit and truth he will show, and with shadows cast away we shall be illumined by the truth. I am he who am speaking with thee. Know that he whom you await as to come has come; and with a husband brought with you to rule you, labor to learn what is necessary to faith. And because she already knew who could teach her, though she did not yet recognize him as he was teaching her, she was worthy that he should manifest himself to her, whence he says: I am the Messias; having received this manifestation she has nothing further to seek, whence follows: The woman therefore left her water-pot, etc. But the Evangelist interposes something about the disciples.
4.27: 4.27 And they wondered that. They did not wonder that he speaks with a woman, for he was accustomed to speak with women, but that he speaks with a foreigner, ignorant of the mystery of the Church to come from the Gentiles. And they suspect no evil, but marvel at his clemency, that he teaches an erring Gentile, as one who came to seek that which was lost.
4.28: 4.28 The woman therefore left. Having heard I am he, the woman, now having in her understanding Christ the head of the husband, left the water-pot, that is, cupidity, and ran to preach the gospel. Here let those about to preach the gospel learn first to lay aside the care and burden of this world.
4.29: 4.29 Come, and see. Step by step she leads those uninstructed ones to the truth; and she does not at once affirm Christ, lest they be angered and indignant.
4.33: 4.33 Hath any man brought him to eat? They did not dare to question the Lord, fearing lest they be rebuked by him if they questioned incautiously.
4.34: 4.34 My meat is. They did not understand the food, just as the woman above did not understand the water, whence the master instructs them not by a roundabout way as he did her, but now openly, saying: My meat is to do, etc. The will of him. Of the Father. The will of the Father is that he be believed in, that is, the Son whom he himself sent. The work of the Father is our salvation. Therefore the food of Christ is our faith and our salvation. He does the will, therefore, by teaching men to believe in him; he does the work by bringing the mystery of redemption to maturity.
4.35: 4.35 Do not you say. Since he seeks the faith and salvation of the peoples, he is fervent for the work and is determined to send laborers. Lift up your eyes. Consider with the understanding of the mind that, winter having passed, that is, unbelief, the warmth of faith is present and hearts are ready, that you may gather from them the works of justice; as if to say: Help in fulfilling the will of the Father. And you well can, because the harvest is ready, that is, see the Gentiles believing easily.
4.36: 4.36 That both he that soweth. Both were needed, sower and reaper, because in this the saying is shown to be approved, that one soweth, and another reapeth; for unless they had been made ready by the prophets, they would not have heard the apostles.
4.38: 4.38 I have sent you. I make you reapers there where others sowed, that is, in Judea, where the first crop was gathered, whence some going out sowed in the whole world, from which another harvest, as it were, rises from the grains, to be gathered at the end of the world by angels as reapers. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labors. For many were the labors of the patriarchs and prophets, in all of which there was prophecy of Christ, and they suffered much, as in the cold of sowing-time.
4.40: 4.40 So when they were come. First they heard the report, afterward they beheld him present, and it is not enough for them, but they make him stay with them, that they might be instructed by his own words, which they prefer to the words of the woman. In all of which, by contrast, the hardness of the Jews is reproved, who do not believe even miracles. And he abode there two days. Morally: so daily among those who are outside, Christ is announced through the woman, that is, the Church, and they believe through this report. Thence he abides with them for two days without mention of night, that their light may be instructed by the two precepts of charity.
4.42: 4.42 And they said to the woman. After the Lord, by the presence of the flesh, had poured the grace of his knowledge into the Jews spiritually instructed, into the woman, that is, the law, they said, we now believe not for thy saying.
4.43: 4.43 For we ourselves have heard. Because, having first stayed in his own country, he had worked miracles, yet only a few believed in him; whence, on seeing the sign, his disciples believed in him, not others; and therefore from the Samaritans, who easily believed without seeing any sign, he returns to these, that those who did not believe through the earlier things may now believe. It signifies that from the Gentiles easily converted, at the end of the world he will return to the Jews, who are his own country, because he had not had honor among them before.
4.44: 4.44 For a prophet. Allegorically: the country of Christ is the people of the Jews, where he is without honor, because few of them believe what is said of the Galileans, the fellow citizens of Christ. The Church of the Gentiles, easily believing, is like the Samaritans, and these many by the word of preaching alone, those few by miracles. Behold why he came; therefore he returns, because he testified that a prophet hath no honor in his own country; otherwise it seems he should not have returned to these, where he has no honor, but remained with those among whom he was well received.
4.46: 4.46 And there was a certain ruler, whose son. This ruler can figure some teacher of the Jewish nation, who at last, after the full conversion of the Church of the Gentiles, to which the Lord, expelled by the Jews, passed over through the disciples, prays for his son, the Jewish people, whom he knows will receive faith only at the end of the world, that he may be healed of the long sickness of perfidy.
4.47: 4.47 And he besought him. Already believing that he could heal his son, but because he does not believe that through the deity, which is everywhere, he is present to the son, he asks that he come down and heal by his bodily presence, whence he is rebuked for infidelity: Unless you see signs and wonders, etc. In contrast the centurion is praised, who says: Say the word only, and my servant shall be healed Matth. 8.; whence: I have not found so great faith in Israel. Or perhaps he desired to test what sort of man Christ was, whence he is rebuked: Unless you see signs and wonders. For the salvation of his son he himself believed, and his whole house.
4.48: 4.48 Unless you see signs. In this he is rebuked for unbelief, because he did not believe that he is everywhere, and by his hardness is signified the hardness of the Jews, who do not believe even when they have seen miracles. Truly, on the other hand, by Samaria is signified the faith of the Gentiles, which believed by the word alone; and this, as far as the allegory goes, will last from the first coming of Christ until after the reign of Antichrist among the perfidious Jews. And wonders. Prodigium is said as though porro dictum, as being something which signifies something. Or, prodigium as though procul a digito, because it prefigures something remote and future.
4.49: 4.49 Come down. As though he could not heal otherwise unless he were present. Whence the Lord, showing that he is not absent where he is invited, heals by command alone, whence: Go thy way, thy son. He does not go to the son of the ruler, lest he seem to honor riches; he promises to go to the servant of the centurion, he who does not despise the nature of man: in this he destroys pride, which in men does not weigh the nature but the things that are outwardly visible. Himself believed. Not the other citizens, in which the fewness of the faith of the Jews is signified, although they had seen signs, whence he adds: This again is the second sign that Jesus did. Just as above the multitude of the Gentiles to be converted by the word alone was signified in the Samaritans.
4.54: 4.54 This again is the second miracle that Jesus did, when he was come out of Judea into Galilee. Of all the miracles which Jesus did in the year before the death of John, John makes no mention except of these, and of the disputation of Christ with the Jews, which is placed above. For the other Evangelists have plainly told what he here passes over in silence.
5.4: 5.4 And an angel. Behold two miracles: one invisibly by an angel in the pool, the other visibly by the Lord. In each one was healed, that unity may be commended. Otherwise it would not have been great in power and little in kindness that one of so many should be healed by him who could raise up all with one word. But in these bodily things he aims more at the eternal salvation of souls.
5.5: 5.5 Thirty-eight. That is, forty less two, which number consists of four times ten, and signifies the perfection of works, in the ten precepts of the law and the four Gospels, from which he has two less who lacks the charity of God and neighbor.
5.6: 5.6 Wilt thou be made whole? He is not ignorant of what he wants, but he kindles love of health, of which he already despaired, whence he was already complaining that he had no one to put him into the water.
5.8: 5.8 Take up thy bed. Love your neighbor by bearing his infirmities, since he bore you patiently when you were infirm, and be solicitous not only for your own raising up in years but also for the salvation of your neighbors. Behold the angel of great counsel, hidden in the flesh, when the water of the Jews was troubled, made one man whole.
5.9: 5.9 And he walked. By loving God hasten even to the vision of him, neither deserting for love of him the brother to whom you are going, nor ceasing because of the brother from seeking him.
5.10: 5.10 The Jews therefore said. The Jews, observers of the letter, not knowing the grace by which the law is fulfilled, which commands to cease from every servile work, that is, from sin, whence here it is said: Take up thy bed, etc. It is not lawful. They do not slander about health, those who in the sabbath care for animals, but about the carrying of the bed.
5.11: 5.11 He answered them. He does not yield to those who object, but, obedient to the commands of the healer, he sets the authority of his healing against those who slander.
5.13: 5.13 Knew not who it was. Placed in the crowd he did not recognize Jesus, but afterward in the temple. In which we are taught that whoever wishes to attain the vision of God should flee the crowd of his own affections and the wickedness of men, and go to the temple of interior prayer.
5.14: 5.14 In the temple. Not in the crowd, but in the temple, because if we wish to know the grace of the creator, we must flee gatherings and become a temple. Sin no more. He hints that he was sick on account of his sins, but Jesus himself healed him within as without, whence he forewarns him lest by sinning again he be judged more severely.
5.16: 5.16 Because he did these things on the sabbath. As though acting as a dissolver of the law, against God who rested on the sabbath, having first worked six days. Against which Jesus says: God did not work only six days, as you suppose, but worketh until now, because he who in six days made new things, from which he rested on the seventh day, afterward works until the end by governing, sustaining, renewing, propagating, that the things made may endure. And since God always works, it is certain that what is read of the sabbath rest is a sacrament.
5.17: 5.17 But Jesus answered. As if to say: Blind ones in the law, why do you envy me if I heal a man on the sabbath, I who as God with the Father always work?
5.18: 5.18 Jesus therefore answered. Because they were moved on hearing the equality of him whom they think a mere man with God the Father, he adds that he is the Son equal to the Father, of the same will, the same power, the same operation. In discussing these matters he uses this way of speaking by which the minds of little ones can be roused, even if not filled, and by which the minds of adults are exercised and fed. For he says of the deity of the Son: The Son cannot do anything of himself, but what he seeth the Father doing, and the Father showeth him, all of which are not to be taken according to the letter, as it happens among men, but mystically. And he speaks these secret things so that they may be disturbed, or that perhaps, being disturbed, they may seek a physician. Also for our sake, that they might be written for us, which, not well understood, would lead into error, well understood, into truth.
5.19: 5.19 Amen, amen I say unto you. Here he treats of his identity with the Father, and of his inferiority according to the man, and of what he does in these, namely both resurrections, that of the body and that of the soul. The Son cannot. I am equal to the Father in such a way that he is not from me, but I am from him. He does not do of himself, nor can he of himself, who is not of himself, but he does and can from him from whom he is. These the Son also. It seems that the body does everything the mind does, but not in like manner, since the mind commands the body; but the Father and the Son do the same things and in like manner, because there is one nature, one substance of the Father and the Son, and one will, and one power, and one operation.
5.20: 5.20 Showeth him all things. For the Father to show the Son is to do all things through the Son, so that the Father and the Son may be held equally in our faith. And lest anything less be thought of the Son, he adds: And greater works than these will he show him, that is, through him he will do greater things. What are they? For as the Father raiseth up the dead and giveth life. It is greater to raise the dead than to heal a sick man, which was the matter at hand. Greater works than these. The Father raises souls through the Son, that souls may live from the substance of the Father and the Son, and to that Son made man in time he will show greater things, that is, the resurrection of bodies, that you may wonder that it is done through the Son.
5.21: 5.21 For as the Father raiseth up. He begins to show what the Son does according as he is equal to the Father, namely that he raises souls from death. And this is the first resurrection, from vices. In what follows he shows also the resurrection of dead bodies, according as he is the Son of man, and hath given him power, that is, to the Son. So the Son also. AUG. Because the Father and the Son are the same life. He judges and raises bodies, etc., up to this reason is given, because he is the Son of man.
5.23: 5.23 That all men may honor. He honors God who commends the Creator as omnipotent, eternal. He honors the Father who believes that he has a Son equal to himself. He honors the Son who believes him to be equal to the Father. He who honoreth not. AUG. For if the Son were believed to be less, the Father would be dishonored, because either out of envy he would not have wished to beget him equal, or being weak he could not, and so he would be convicted of not being God, because powerless.
5.24: 5.24 Because he that, etc. Because I am equal to the Father and to be honored with one honor with him, therefore he who heareth my word, that is, who believes me to be the Son and believes him to be the Father, hath life everlasting, because this is life everlasting, as he will say later, that they may know thee, whom I sent, Jesus Christ, to be the one true God. Hears and believes. Why does he say: Heareth my word and believeth, not me, but him that sent me: because his word is in me, indeed I am his word. He who believes him, therefore, believes his word, that is, me. But is passed. Here, from the death of infidelity to the life of faith and justice; afterward, from corruption to eternity. Of the first resurrection he adds more openly: Amen, amen I say unto you, that the hour cometh, and now is, etc.
5.25: 5.25 That the hour cometh. I said that the Son raises and gives life, which is true, because the hour cometh, etc., and the manifestation of his Father; for here it is about the raising of the soul from sins. The voice of the Son. This is fitting only for the just, who so hear of his incarnation that they believe he is the Son of God. For as the Father. AUG. The life which is the Father himself and the Son pertains to the soul, not to the body, etc., up to life, and the same is the life of the body. In himself. Not from elsewhere, but he himself is life, so the Son also is life in himself. But they differ, because the Father is life without being born, the Son is life by being born of the Father, whence he says: He hath given; not that the Son was ever without life, but life is born of him; therefore he gave, that is, life begot life.
5.27: 5.27 And hath given him power. After speaking of the resurrection of the soul, he adds the resurrection of the flesh. And the power which the Son has with the Father in secret, the Father gave him, because he is the Son of man, in which form he will be seen judging good and bad. For the vision of the form of God is promised only to the clean of heart, whence: Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God Matth. 5. AUG. Christ in that he is the Son of God, etc., up to by the Word made flesh, the Son of man, the resurrection of bodies takes place.
5.28: 5.28 For the hour cometh. As above he is the author of the resurrection of the mind to eternal life, so here too he is the author of the resurrection of the flesh; otherwise no one would believe.
5.30: 5.30 I cannot of myself do anything. He gave me power of judgment, yet I cannot of myself, that is, he who is not of himself does not act of himself, and so he who blames him for the work on the sabbath blames the Father. As I hear. I hear by unity of substance, that is, I know, because to hear is nothing other than to know or to be. Or, I, the Son of man, can do nothing of myself, but as I hear from God I judge, and this my judgment, whatever it concerns, is just, because I seek not my own will, that is, of man, but the will of the Father, which concerns the salvation of men, who sent me for this, that is, caused me to be incarnate. I seek not. He speaks now according as he is equal to the Father, that true deity may be proved in him, now according as he is less, that true humanity may be proved.
5.31: 5.31 If I bear witness. I speak of the identity of his essence with the Father, from which live not bodies, which do not feel, but rational souls, intermediate between God and bodies; having also spoken of the lesser state of his humanity, in which he dies, rises, raises bodies and judges; he adds concerning his testimonies, which he does not need to have from man, because he has them from the works which the Father gave and from the Father himself. Yet he has them also from men, but as from lamps, that is, from John and from Moses, who, if they cannot join souls to God, can nevertheless refute enemies.
5.34: 5.34 But I say these things. But nevertheless I bring in the testimony of John, that through John you men may be led to the truth itself, and believing may be saved.
5.35: 5.35 He was, etc. He who showed me outwardly visible to the eyes of men, inwardly kindles the hearts of men to know me. All the prophets and apostles also are lamps: Christ is the true light, which enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world.
5.37: 5.37 Neither have you heard his voice. Even if you suppose that on Sinai you heard his voice and saw his shape.
