5.41: 5.41 Glory. Nor do I say this to seek my own glory, but I grieve with you who are in error, who have not the love of God, and I wish to lead you back to the way of truth.
5.42: 5.42 That you have not the love. The love of God is not in you, because you receive me not, that is, you do not believe, because I came that the Father might be glorified through me.
5.43: 5.43 If another. Antichrist, who seeks his own glory, not God's, that is, will come in his own name; this is what the Apostle says, that they may believe lying, who did not believe the truth.
6.1: 6.1 Over the sea. Tiberias and Capharnaum are on the same shore on our side; beyond, on the other, opposite shore, is the place where this miracle was done. It is not properly called a sea, but a certain great overflow of the Jordan.
6.2: 6.2 And a great multitude followed him. This miracle having been seen, a great crowd of Gentiles follows, because just as he restored inwardly in spirit those whom he healed of bodily infirmity, so he healed them of the disease of unbelief.
6.5: 6.5 When Jesus therefore had lifted up his eyes. By his example he admonishes us to lift up the eyes of our heart, so that if perhaps under his leading we are permitted to ascend to the height of action and knowledge, the crowd of carnal thoughts following may not disturb us, nor cast us down from the height of contemplation, but that we may take care to feed it with spiritual food, as far as it can take.
6.7: 6.7 Two hundred. The hundred doubled signifies the perfection of good action and rational knowledge, which are not sufficient for those to be instructed in the faith unless the height of theology be added to them, which leads souls purged by good operation and enlightened by knowledge of created things to the complete fullness of spiritual refreshments.
6.9: 6.9 There is a boy here. This boy is Moses the lawgiver, whose law led no one to perfection. One, because he prefigured the vanity of the future Church. Here, that is, in the Old Testament, which, although it now grows worthless as the New shines forth, has nevertheless not yet wholly withdrawn. But what, etc. As if to say: What do the letter of the law or bodily senses profit for the multitude of those believing in you, who are going to ask for spiritual nourishment, which surpasses every letter and every bodily sense?
6.10: 6.10 Make the men sit down. The master of truth first instructed his hearers in the simplicity of the letter, as in the lowest places, and in the simplicity of visible creation, so that they might thus be lifted up to the height of contemplation.
6.14: 6.14 Those men therefore, when they had seen what, etc. They were advancing with faith not yet full, and so they did not know how to call him God. We, more certain than they, say: This is the Word, without whom there is no prophet or angel.
6.15: 6.15 Jesus therefore. Those who wish to seize him and make him king signify the disciples and other believers, who wish to anticipate the time of his kingdom, supposing that he came in such a way that he was already reigning. But at this time the kingdom is being gathered, which will be manifest at the end, when he will say: Come, possess you the kingdom prepared for you. He fled, therefore, not fearing to be held, he who afterward converses with the same people, but wishing to signify that his height cannot be understood. He fled into the mountain, that is, he ascended the heavens, the sole priest interceding for the people placed outside, who meanwhile is tossed by the waves, whence he adds: And when evening was come. The evening of the world is after the ascension of Christ, in which the disciples go down to the labors of the world and steer the ship, that is, the Church.
6.19: 6.19 They were afraid. That the disciples, who bore the figure of all those who were to be in the Church, on seeing the Lord coming to them upon the waves of the sea were afraid, and, as another evangelist says more openly, thought him a phantom, is not without mystery, because even today many in the Church, when they hear themselves persuaded to give up present and perishable goods in exchange for whatever eternal things are to be held, are afraid and believe themselves deceived; to them the Lord says: Fear not, it is I.
6.22: 6.22 The next day. This miracle was made known to the crowd, that Jesus had walked upon the waters, because there had been only one boat there, and Jesus had not entered it with his disciples; how then had the crossing been made, unless he had walked upon the waters?
6.25: 6.25 And when they had found. Behold, he is present to those from whom he had fled, lest they make him king. Why then had he fled, if not for the sake of the aforesaid sacrament? Again present he speaks to them, that he may satisfy the minds of those whose bellies he had filled, saying: Amen, amen I say to you, teaching those whom he appointed as teachers to flee praise and earthly dominion, yet to press on with preaching.
6.26: 6.26 Amen, amen I say to you. After he had treated of his divinity, by which he is the same as the Father and to be honored with the same honor, and of his humanity, by which he frees from death and raises up and is worthy of great honor, he wishes to treat of the food of life, that is, the word of God. And this is the connection as to the sense. According to the letter, however, it is thus: You seek me, not for my own sake, but for the loaves that perish. Therefore labor, that is, seek me for my own sake, not for anything else. For he is that food which endureth unto life everlasting, as he will openly say afterward. Likewise many daily seek Jesus, not for Jesus' sake, but that it may go well with them in time.
6.27: 6.27 Him hath God sealed. As if by a proper sign he has distinguished him from the rest, because he who is the Son of man is also the Son of God, and therefore do not despise me as the Son of man, but ask of me spiritual food.
6.29: 6.29 This is the work of God. Faith working through love is a work, because if the ability is lacking, nothing but the will is required. Rightly also faith which worketh by charity is called a work, which is the beginning and end of all good.
6.32: 6.32 He said therefore. Since they were preferring the work of Moses to his own work, he shows that it is less, because it was not bread from heaven, but only a figure of it, and his own is greater, who is the bread from heaven which gives life, and this is the food which above he said endureth unto life everlasting.
6.33: 6.33 For the bread of God is that. The angels eat the pure Word, solid food; we, however, the Word turned into milk, because if we cannot eat, we can suck. For unless he were incarnate, he would not be known by us, would not be tasted by us.
6.34: 6.34 Lord, give us always, etc. As the Samaritan woman, hearing: Whosoever shall drink of this water shall not thirst for ever, understood it according to the body, and yet, wishing to be free of labor and need, said: Give me this water, so these seek a bread that will refresh them and never fail, on account of which they wished to make him king. But Jesus recalls them to himself and opens more evidently what bread he spoke of, I am the bread of life. I shall be able to give life, because I am the life-giving bread, baked and formed by the fire of the Holy Spirit in the oven of the virginal womb, and given to the world to drive away the hunger of ignorance of God.
6.36: 6.36 But I said to you. As if to say: I did not speak of this bread as one who knows that you are to be filled, but as a reproach for your unbelief, because you see and believe not.
6.37: 6.37 All that the Father giveth me, etc. That is, whatever the Father draws to me, the Father gives to the Son. The Father draws to the Son those who believe in the Son for this reason, that they believe he has God for Father. Shall come. The humble is united to me, the humble one; and therefore he is not cast out, which belongs only to the proud, who has nothing in good within, neither here nor in the future.
6.39: 6.39 Now this is the will of him that sent me, the Father, etc. It is not the will of God that one of the little ones should perish; from the swelling ones he perishes, from the little ones nothing. I should lose nothing, etc. That is, because he sees me and believes in me, who am life as the Father also is, and therefore he now has life, which is not his only, but I will also raise him up.
6.40: 6.40 That every one, etc. Above he said: He that heareth my word and believeth him that sent me; here it is said: He that seeth the Son and believeth in him. He does not say: He that believeth in the Father, because to believe in the Son is the same as to believe in the Father, since as the Father hath life in himself, so also the Son hath life in himself.
6.41: 6.41 The Jews therefore murmured. Not knowing this bread, nor his heavenly Father, because, puffed up with their own justice, in which they presume on their own strength, they do not hunger for the justice of God which comes from heaven.
6.43: 6.43 Murmur not. As though I were not the bread that came down from heaven, for truly I am, but no man can come to me except he be drawn by the Father, and therefore you do not believe me to be from the Father, because you are not drawn by the Father.
6.44: 6.44 Except the Father. AUG. The Father draws to the Son him who therefore believes in the Son because he considers, etc., up to in which a great grace is commended. And I will raise him up, etc. I, equal to the Father, will make him see what he believes, eat what he hungers for, have what he loved and desired, which cannot be in the present, where he is only drawn.
6.45: 6.45 It is written. Truly no man cometh to me unless the Father teach him, because so the prophecies attest. All men of that kingdom, that is, of the Christian faith, shall be taught of God, because although men speak outwardly, God alone opens the understanding within, instructs within by knowledge and love of the truth; thus whoever hears and learns of the Father cometh to me. In the prophets. He says 'prophets' in the plural, because all the prophets, filled with one and the same spirit, although they prophesied different things, nevertheless tended to the same end.
6.46: 6.46 Not that any man hath seen the Father, etc. That is, I know the Father, because I am from him, and therefore believe, because he that believeth in me hath life everlasting. He could have said, has me, but he reveals that he himself is life everlasting, because the Word is the life of men, which to his own flesh also, which he had taken up, to which death came in order that he might take death away, he gives life in the resurrection, and to others believing in him.
6.48: 6.48 I am the bread of life. Your fathers, etc. The manna of which you are proud, to your murmuring fathers whose sons you are, was not by their murmuring the bread of life, because they did not understand in it the spiritual food, and so also you who hear me do not understand spiritually. But Moses and other elect lived by the manna, because they ate spiritually. So also do those who now receive my words spiritually. I am the bread of life. Behold, he covers the sacrament with words, so that the Jews and even some disciples not believing his words may be more scandalized, and the humble apostles believing humbly may be proved; whence Peter: Thou hast the words of eternal life.
6.52: 6.52 And the bread, etc. How he is bread he determines not only according to the Word by which all things live, but also according to the flesh assumed for the life of the world. For human flesh, which was liable to sin and therefore dead, united to his clean flesh, incorporated, made one with him, lives by his spirit, as a body lives by its spirit; but he who is not of the body of Christ does not live by the spirit of Christ. But because the Jews were not of this unity, they contended; nor is it explained to such persons how the Lord gives his flesh to eat, but they heard it, whence they are the more moved.
6.54: 6.54 Unless you eat the flesh, etc. AUG. He wishes this food and drink to be understood as fellowship, etc., up to that from many grains there is one bread, and from many grapes wine flows together.
6.55: 6.55 He that eateth. Some saints explain this of the eating at the altar, and they say well, but they ask how it comes to be unto life everlasting, since for some it is unto death, as the Apostle says. If anyone eats at the altar with this eating of which he treats here, namely with faith working and with love, he eats unto life everlasting. But if anyone otherwise, unto death.
6.56: 6.56 For my flesh. Truly soul and body will live from this food, because my flesh is meat indeed. It alone makes men immortal, so that they shall neither hunger nor thirst; another food does not afford this, even if it is sought in it.
6.57: 6.57 He that eateth. Now he explains how what he said comes about, and what it is to eat the flesh and drink the blood, namely to abide in Christ and to have Christ abiding in oneself. But he who does not abide in Christ, and in whom Christ does not abide, does not eat spiritually, and so receives the sacrament bodily for himself unto judgment.
6.58: 6.58 As the living Father hath sent me. He sent me, equal to himself, that is, made me man, and hence it is that I refer my life to him as to a greater. And he that eateth me, the same also shall live. That I live from the Father, my self-emptying brings about; that man live from me, the participation brings about, which eats me.
6.59: 6.59 This is the bread. And so it is clear that this is truly the bread from heaven, not manna, because the fathers who ate that, like you, died forever; the man who had not life, eating this bread, shall live for ever. Above he had said, I am the bread which came down from heaven. Here he says: This, that is, the Son of man, to eat whose flesh I invite, is that bread which came down from heaven: therefore the Son of man and the Son of God are the same.
6.61: 6.61 Many therefore. Many, carnally wise, as though he promised to distribute to them in pieces the flesh in which he was clothed, think it contrary to nature that he should give human flesh as food for men. This saying is hard, etc. AUG. It was fitting that it be said thus, so that it might not be understood by men, but the secret of God be covered with words: the secret of God ought to make them attentive, not hostile.
6.63: 6.63 If then, etc. The sentence is left suspended. As if to say: Then you will understand that I do not distribute my body in the way you suppose, and that this grace is not consumed by bites, but by giving myself to them by spiritual grace I convert them into my body; from this he plainly resolves what had moved them; for they thought that he would distribute his body, while he says that he will ascend into heaven, certainly whole. What therefore is to be held he openly adds:
6.64: 6.64 It is the spirit that quickeneth. The flesh, as you understand it, like what is bought in the market, like any other food, profits nothing; yet the same flesh, the vessel of the spirit who works salvation in it, profits much, just as knowledge alone puffs up, yet it is not itself evil, but through charity edifies. The words that I, etc. By which I said that I am to be eaten, that men abide in me and I in them. That anyone abide in Christ as a member, and Christ in him as in a temple, unity effects. Unity, however, is from charity, and charity from the spirit; therefore the spirit that quickeneth does not separate the members knit together.
6.65: 6.65 But there are some, etc. The Prophet: Unless you believe, you shall not understand: through faith we are joined, through understanding we are given life. And who he was that would betray him. Because Judas withdraws among the scandalized, yet remains to lie in wait, he neither keeps silent about him nor openly points him out, that all may fear while one perishes.
6.66: 6.66 That no man can, etc. He adds the reason why some do not believe: Because it is not given by God; for faith is not from men of themselves, as their own, but from God, as grace.
6.67: 6.67 From this time, etc. Note that one must speak cautiously, but if nevertheless anyone is scandalized by your words, he has consolation in him by whose saying many were scandalized, who did this to be an example for you.
6.71: 6.71 Have not I chosen you, etc. Twelve is a sacred number which remains, even though Judas perishes from it. He chose eleven to remain, he chose Judas that through him the dispensation of divine mercy for the salvation of the world might be fulfilled, using evil for good, as the wicked use the goods of God for evil.
7.1: 7.1 After these things. The Lord, remaining in the flesh, frequently walked in Galilee, so that those wishing to imitate him may learn to pass over from vices to virtues: which that figured. Or that the saints of that time might await the passage of the word of God from Judea to the Gentiles.
7.2: 7.2 The feast day. Not that it is one, for there are seven, but according to their custom, however many there are, they are called as one on account of one festivity, scenopegia, the feast of tabernacles, because in the seventh month the Jews dwelt in tabernacles, in memory of those in which their fathers dwelt in the desert.
7.3: 7.3 That thy disciples also. The works which true disciples knew should be extolled by divine praises and not by popular favor.
7.4: 7.4 For there is no man. They take thought for his glory. As though: You do wonderful things, namely in secret, but become known, that you may be praised by all.
7.6: 7.6 Time. Therefore my time is not yet come, but yours is, because I am not a lover of the world as you are, but its accuser, and so the world, which is yours, does not listen to you, its false witnesses, who call good evil and evil good.
7.8: 7.8 I go not up. AUG. Some say this pertains to the passion, because he ascends the cross not at the feast of scenopegia, but at the Paschal feast, in which the lamb is wont to be slain.
7.10: 7.10 Not openly, etc. Typically: Christ goes up to the feast hidden, because in all those figures he lay hidden who is now manifest to us. And that he hid is an example for avoiding the wicked: that he speaks openly and is not seized by those who sought him is of power.
7.16: 7.16 Jesus answered them: My doctrine is not mine, a man's, but God's. Or because the Word is not of no one, but his doctrine belongs to someone, that is, he himself is the Word, his doctrine is not his own, but his from whom he is: which is, I am not of myself. And because he saw that not all would understand this depth, he gave counsel: If you wish to understand, believe. This is: If any man believes me to be the Son of God, he shall know of the doctrine, that is, he will understand that my doctrine is not mine.
7.18: 7.18 He that speaketh of himself. Antichrist is not true, and injustice is in him, because he seeks his own glory, not God's, by whom he is not sent, but permitted to come. But he that, etc. That is, I, who although equal to the Father yet in the form of a servant seek the glory of the Father, not my own; in this he gives an example of humility, that we ascribe all good things to God.
7.19: 7.19 Did not Moses, etc. I speak from God and seek his glory, true, just: but you who glory in the law, against the law which forbids to kill, seek to kill me.
7.20: 7.20 Thou hast a devil. They seek to kill, and, what is worse, say that he has a devil, who drives out devils.
7.21: 7.21 One work I have done. You wonder at one; what if you saw them all? It was one work, that he healed the whole man on the sabbath, whence the foolish observers of the sabbath were troubled, but Moses convicts them, commanding to circumcise on the eighth day, which sometimes happens to fall on the sabbath. And this is: Therefore let no one be troubled if salvation is always done even on the sabbath. And let all know that things which pertain to salvation ought always to be done.
7.22: 7.22 Circumcision. ALC. Circumcision was given for three causes. First, etc., up to and the heart is stripped of desires.
7.23: 7.23 If a man receive circumcision, etc. As though you who glory in the law, against the law which announces me, plot about my death, but it is not against the law that I, the Lord of the sabbath, made the whole man whole on the sabbath. For the keeping of the sabbath, like all other things, is for the salvation of man, as you yourselves, circumcising on the sabbath (because it pertains to salvation), do not believe you break the sabbath.
7.24: 7.24 Judge not, etc. You ought not to be angry with me over the saving of a man on the sabbath, as you are not angry over circumcision on the sabbath, because one must not judge according to the face, that is, the action of persons, so that what was lawful for Moses is not lawful for me, but with just judgment, that is, according to the truth of things: which being known, you will condemn neither me nor Moses, nor say that I am contrary to him. In this he rebukes them, and instructs us not to accept persons in judging cases, not that we should not honor persons differently according to the diversity of ranks.
7.25: 7.25 Some therefore said. Because although he went up to the feast hidden, he speaks openly, and the power appears which had been thought timidity. Some wonder, because he is not seized by power, whose death was so eagerly sought, and not yet fully understanding that the power is his, they suppose it is the knowledge of the rulers, because they have known him to be the Christ, whence they object to themselves that this is not the Christ, since no man knoweth whence Christ is, because although the place of his birth and the like is told by the prophets, yet his eternal birth is born of the Father, whence the Prophet: Who shall declare his generation? Isa. 53. Hence Christ answers to both, both concerning infirmity and concerning majesty.
7.28: 7.28 And you know me. That is, the likeness of my face, and whence I am, my birth and parents, which is: you know me according to the flesh, but not according to the Divinity, because I am not come of myself. They did not know that he was the Son of God, nor sent by the Father; they did not know God the Father either, who is the true begetter of the very truth. But whence they can know, he adds: I know him. Therefore ask of me, believe in me, because no one knoweth the Father but the Son, and he to whom the Son will reveal him. Mark 11.
7.29: 7.29 But I know him. Therefore I know him, because I am from him, etc. Let him briefly embrace both: I am from him, because the Son is of the Father, the Father not of another, and you see me in the flesh, because he sent me. In this is the great authority of the begetter, and a nature common with men.
7.30: 7.30 His hour. Not that there is a necessity of the deed, but the opportuneness of the will. For he willed to be born at an opportune time, after a long series of heralds sent before. Similarly the preacher of the Gospel willed to die at an opportune time.
7.32: 7.32 The Pharisees heard. The senseless rulers, having heard the murmuring by which Christ was glorified by the crowd, seek to kill him, whom nevertheless they could not seize while he was unwilling, but they heard him teaching.
7.33: 7.33 Yet a little while. As if to say: What you now wish, you will do afterward, but not now, because yet a little while I am with you, in which I must fulfil my dispensation, and then I go to him that sent me, then I must suffer. And you who now do not wish to hear him present and working miracles will seek me after the resurrection and ascension, when so many miracles shall be done by the apostles by my power, and when so great a multitude shall believe. For then, pricked at so great a crime as the death of Christ, they said to Peter: What shall we do? I am with you and I go. He does not say I shall be, but I am, because although according as he is man he changes places, according as he is God he does not change, since he is everywhere. Hence elsewhere: The Son of man who is in heaven, as if he says it while speaking on earth.
7.34: 7.34 You cannot come. He does not say you will not be able, but you cannot. For such they then were, who could not; as he also says elsewhere to Peter: Thou canst not follow me now, but thou shalt follow hereafter John 13.; so neither is despair given of these.
7.35: 7.35 Among themselves, etc. Whence they did not know how to speak to the Lord, and yet, not knowing, they pronounced that which was to be. Which, though not by presence through the apostles, yet he is about to go to the Gentiles who will believe.
7.36: 7.36 What is this? Since in ignorance they had prophesied the truth, by repeating the same question they show that they prophesied out of ignorance, so that they seem rather to have been ignorant than to have prophesied.
7.37: 7.37 And on the last day. After the dissensions of the Jews about Jesus, and after the words he said, by which some were hardened, others taught, on the last day of the scenopegia he calls, not only speaking but crying out, that he who thirsts may come to him. If any man thirst. Let him drink the Spirit, as he afterward explains, and when he has drunk, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water. The belly is the conscience of the heart, which, purified by drinking the Spirit, lives and has a fountain. And it is itself the fountain or river, which flows with benevolence, while it wishes to look to the neighbor's good; he who thinks his good things suffice for himself alone was not that fountain. HIER. Boldly and with all freedom I declare, from that time, etc., up to wherefore, when Jesus was led to his passion, they deny and swear that they do not know Christ.
7.39: 7.39 For as yet, etc. Although the prophets received the same spirit, and John and others before the resurrection of Christ, yet there was to be another mode of donation, more open and fuller: for after the resurrection, when he first appeared to the apostles, he breathed on their face, he who by a breath put the soul into the first man and raised him from the clay. Signifying therefore that he is the same, he breathed the Spirit upon the apostles, that they might rise from the mire. Then after the ascension he sent the Spirit more fully in fiery tongues, that they might teach all nations, as they then in all tongues: so now the unity of the Church speaks in all tongues, and he who is cut off from that unity has not the spirit. Because Jesus was not yet glorified, etc. From that crowd, therefore, etc. But after they are baptized with the Holy Spirit, and the grace of the Holy Spirit is poured out on them, then they speak freely to the rulers of the Jews: We ought to obey God rather than men Acts 5.; they raise the dead, rejoice among scourges, shed blood, and are crowned with other torments. Not yet, therefore, was the Spirit in the apostles, nor did spiritual graces flow from their belly, because the Lord was not yet glorified.
7.45: 7.45 The servants therefore came. Those sent to seize him returned free from guilt, full of admiration, witnesses of the divine doctrine.
7.47: 7.47 Are you also, etc. Those who, leaving the evil of unbelief, had passed over to faith had been seduced in a praiseworthy way.
7.48: 7.48 Hath any one of the rulers, etc. Those who teach the law despise him who sent the law, but those who had not known the law believe in him who gave the law, that what is said may be fulfilled: That they who see not may see, and they who see may become blind John 9.
7.51: 7.51 Doth our law. Because those perverse ones wished to be condemners before being investigators, but this man thought that if they heard him patiently when present, perhaps they would be like the servants who preferred to believe than to seize. By the authority of the law, therefore, he wishes to induce them to be willing to hear him first.
7.52: 7.52 Art thou also a Galilean, etc. And every man returned, etc. Jesus was called a Galilean because his parents were of Nazareth.
8.1: 8.1 And Jesus. Because it was his custom to teach by day in the temple and in the evening return to Bethany, which is on the Mount of Olives. Mystically: it signifies the height of mercy, whence chrism, that is, anointing, comes to us. In the morning he returns to the temple. Morning is the rising of the new light after the darkness of the law, in which he came to unfold and give his mercy to the faithful, that is, in his temple. Sitting is the humility of the Incarnation, by which he has mercy and teaches, whence the people came to him more willingly, but the enemy Pharisees test him about justice, whether he will speak against it. They knew him to be gentle and a preacher of mercy, whence he pleased the people, whence they thought he would say the adulteress should be dismissed, and in this he would be called an enemy of the law, contrary to Moses and to God its author, and, with the adulteress, guilty of death. But if he said according to the law that she should be stoned, they would deride him, as though he did not have the gentleness he preached and for which he was loved. But he is caught by neither calumny, but, keeping his gentleness, answers what belongs to true justice: He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her. But he does not judge at once, but stooping down with his finger wrote on the ground.
8.3: 8.3 They bring. Mystically: the woman taken in adultery signifies the Synagogue, which adulterated the law of Moses by following the traditions of the fathers. Or which, having left the law of Moses, now follows the faith of Christ, whence the Jew accuses her now as an adulteress. Or it signifies the Church, which, forsaking God, had fornicated with demons, whom the Jew accuses because she comes to Christ, and she was reckoned as a new kind of idolatry.
8.6: 8.6 But Jesus stooping down. What he wrote on the ground, whether their words or something else, is not defined, according as he stoops and writes with his finger. He teaches, however, that before judgment is made we ought to stoop, that is, condescend, in judgment, or make use of discretion in acting.
8.8: 8.8 And again stooping down. When the sentence of justice was given, by which those conscious of evils were struck, he again writes on the ground, as was his custom, turning his face elsewhere, so that it might be free for them to go out, whom he foresaw would go out sooner than ask more questions. He teaches us, however, that as before the correction of another, so also after it, we should humbly examine ourselves, lest the same or something similar be in us.
8.11: 8.11 Neither will I condemn thee. But because she could fear lest he who is without sin should punish her, he says to her, as merciful forgiving past sins: Neither will I condemn thee; as just forbidding her to sin any more.
8.12: 8.12 Again therefore. With the tempters repulsed and the woman's fault healed, he adds more openly what he can do from his Divinity, lest they doubt of that man whether he can forgive sins. I am the light of the world. Which is covered by the cloud of flesh, and thus made bearable to men, whence I can both forgive sins and also enlighten man.
8.13: 8.13 Testimony. They think he is not to be believed. As though: He alone testifies of himself, forgetting the lamps spoken of before, and John the Baptist himself, who showed evidently concerning him.
8.14: 8.14 My testimony is true. My testimony is therefore to be held true, because I know whence I come, that is, because it is confirmed by the testimony of the Father. I came sent by the Father, yet not deserting him, and having fulfilled the ministry I return to the Father, yet I do not leave the world.
8.15: 8.15 You judge according to the flesh. Because you do not know that, therefore you judge according to the flesh, that is, you think me a man, who is not to be believed in his own praise, and you even condemn. I judge not any man. I do not judge as according to the flesh, like us, or I do not judge at all in this first coming, but I save; but because in the second coming he will judge, he adds: And if I do judge, etc.
8.16: 8.16 For I am not alone. AUG. Therefore true, because I am not alone, but I and the Father. Behold, therefore, two in persons, though one in substance; which is: Therefore my judgment is true, because I am the true Son of God, whence it is proved that he is the Son, because he is not alone, but the Father with him.
8.17: 8.17 And in your law it is written. ID. Having spoken of the judgment, that his and the Father's testimony is true, he proves it from the authority of the law. For it is said, etc., up to as Susanna, accused, had.
8.19: 8.19 They said therefore to him. Judging according to the flesh, they understood Christ's Father carnally; but he was man in the open, the Word of the Father in secret. Where is thy Father? As though they say: We see you, but not the Father with you. To whom the answer is given in turn: But neither do you know me, because if you know the man whom you see, you do not know what I am in secret, and therefore you do not know the Father. But if you knew me, which is first, know me, and so you would know the Father, because we are one. Perhaps also the Father, etc. He does not doubt, but as it were mocks and rebukes those who doubt; as a lord to a servant: Perhaps I am your Lord.
8.20: 8.20 These words, etc. Gaza means riches, phylax to keep. Typically: the treasury is the mysteries of the Scriptures, which are in the temple, that is, in Christ. These secrets he opened to the apostles after the resurrection, but in these he now speaks by parables to the Jews who do not understand. And no man laid hands on him. That is, as he spoke of the Divinity.
8.21: 8.21 I go. As if of his own will, and therefore you labor in vain. He goes whither he had come from, and whence he had not departed. You shall seek me, therefore persecuting him taken up into the heavens, not desiring to have him as friends. Whence he foretells them their punishment: You shall die in your sin.
8.22: 8.22 Will he kill himself? Foolish words, as if he spoke of death, they could not follow him to death. He spoke, therefore, not of death, but of the glory to which he was going through death, whence to those carnal ones he adds:
8.23: 8.23 You are from beneath. And therefore you savor of the earth, like the serpent you eat earth.
8.24: 8.24 I said therefore to you. Here he explains what it is to be of this world, that is, to be unbelieving sinners who savor earthly things, whence he explains this to them. For if. But on the other hand he gives hope to those who will believe. You believe. He says you believe, not you perceive, because no one now grasps the immutable essence. I am he; you shall die, etc. He does not say what, whether Christ, or Son of God, or anything of the kind, but to these he uses the word of eternal essence, as once to Moses whom he was sending to free Israel. As if to say: I who sent Moses to free the children of Israel, have come by myself to free the lost. But all other things that are sent, truly are not.
8.25: 8.25 The beginning. AUG. Believe me to be the beginning, etc., up to himself the right hand, the strength, the wisdom, and the Word of the Father. ID. Behold what it is to be, because the beginning abides in itself, renews all things, and cannot be changed. I speak to you. And I have many things to speak to you, by teaching, if you believe, by accusing, if you do not believe, and I who now do not judge but save, have after this to judge. I say have, but all from the Father who is true from himself, from whom I am the truth which he begot from himself, and therefore I say true things, and judge. Behold how he gives glory to the Father, to whom he is equal, to teach us who are lesser to give glory to God.
8.27: 8.27 And they understood not. When he says, he that sent me is true, they did not understand that he spoke of the Father, because they still had closed eyes, and therefore he adds to them: When you shall have lifted up the Son, etc., where he shows that there were some there who after his passion would believe and know who he was.
8.29: 8.29 Because I am. To be is the immutable of the divine substance. But lest he who speaks be understood to be the Father, he adds: And of myself I do nothing; because I am not of myself, but of the Father. Because I, etc. Equality itself is always. Always, not from a certain beginning and thenceforth, but without beginning and end. For the generation of God has no beginning of time, because through the Only-begotten the times were made.
8.30: 8.30 Many believed in him. Faith is to believe what you do not see, truth is to see what you have believed. We do not know in order to believe, but we believe in order to know: therefore Christ, man on earth, lays the foundation of faith, afterward he will give himself to be seen, which is the reward of faith.
8.31: 8.31 Indeed my disciples. To this height you will come by faith, which is humble, and is despised, and is a grain of mustard seed.
8.33: 8.33 Free. The Lord used this word from liberty, not as is commonly said in Latin, that someone is freed from infirmity. And the Lord had not said: you shall be free, but: The truth shall make you free, in which word, however, they understood only carnal liberty. He answered them, etc. Not those who believed, but others in the crowd who did not believe, who, hearing it shall make you free, were indignant at being called servants, thinking he had spoken of carnal liberty. And we have never been slaves to any man. They lie. Joseph served in Egypt, the fathers served in Egypt in clay, these same served the tributes of Caesar. Amen, amen I say, etc. Amen in Hebrew is rendered verum in Latin, which no interpreter has changed, lest, laid bare, it become cheap, but let it have the honor of a secret, and it is as it were an oath, whence Jerome on Isaiah: The Lord swears by himself, since the sentence of his mouth and the word he once uttered he never makes void, that is, he swore by himself.
8.35: 8.35 Now the servant, etc. In this he has terrified us. What hope of liberty, then, is there for those who are not without sin?
8.37: 8.37 I know, etc. The Lord having explained, against those glorying in the vain liberty of the flesh, the true servitude of sin and the true liberty through the Son, conceding to them, namely, that they are sons of Abraham by flesh, shows such free ones not to be sons of Abraham by imitation of faith and justice, but to be sons of the murderer, the devil, seeking to kill him, and so to be truly slaves.
8.39: 8.39 They answered and said to him. Because he reproves them for doing the evil deeds of their father, confessing that their father is Abraham, they provoke him to say some curse against Abraham, so that they may have occasion to do what they wished, but the Lord praises Abraham and condemns these degenerates, saying: If you be the children of Abraham, etc.
8.40: 8.40 But now you seek, etc. He does not say (what he could) that he is the lord of Abraham, lest it be an occasion of calumny, nor the Son of God, but what they envy, and what they can kill.
8.41: 8.41 You do the works. Now he hints at another father than Abraham, whose sons they are, not by nature but by imitation. They said, etc. We, etc. Now understanding that the Lord speaks not of origin of the flesh but of life, and knowing from the usage of the Scriptures that fornication is spoken of spiritually when the soul is subjected to false gods, they change their answer and are now silent about father Abraham, lest it be said to them: Why do you glory in him whose life you do not imitate? And they say God is their Father, wishing to see what he could say to them in reply.
8.42: 8.42 Jesus therefore said. As he showed before about Abraham, so now he shows that God is not their father, because they do not know the Son whom he sent nor love him. For I. The procession from the Father is eternal, in which is the only-begotten Son equal to the Father; he came made man, in which he is a brother to men.
8.43: 8.43 Why do you not know my speech? The matter is as I say, but you cannot know what I say, because you cannot hear, since you are not willing to be corrected by believing. And why this? Because you are of the devil: you have chosen to persevere as sons of the devil.
8.44: 8.44 You are of your father, etc. Behold, now he determines who their father is, whose sons they are not by being born, as the Manichees say, but by imitating; hence it is also said to the Jews: Thy father was an Amorrhite, and thy mother a Cethite Ezech. 16. And the desires. Therefore sons of the devil, because you wish to do the desires of your father, and to kill me in the flesh, because you cannot in the mind. He was a murderer. Note that a murderer is not only one who kills with the sword but also with the word, as the devil killed our first parents, whence in the psalm: Their tongue a sharp sword Psal. 56. And he stood not in the truth. Why did he not stand? Because truth is not in him. That is, the Word and wisdom of the Father. When it is said, in Christ is truth, it is so said that he himself is the truth. If therefore the devil had stood in the truth, he would have stood in Christ, but he did not stand in it, because it is not in him. He speaketh of his own, for he is a liar. And this is not enough, because a man too is a liar who has nothing of his own, but has begun from another, that is, from the devil, therefore he added: And the father thereof. Namely of the lie which he found. Of his own. Because he has not from elsewhere, but from himself after he fell from the truth; whence it is added that he is the father of the lie which he begot from himself, as God the truth from himself.
8.46: 8.46 Which of you, etc. He does not disdain to show by reason that he is not a sinner, etc.
8.48: 8.48 Do not we, etc. Because they were convicted of not being sons of Abraham or of God, but of the devil, they heap on insults, since they could not resist.
8.49: 8.49 I honor. I do what I ought (lest I seem arrogant to you), but you do not do what you ought, because you have not honored me, whom, if you knew him, as I honor the Father, so you would honor me.
8.50: 8.50 But I. Having heard the insult, Thou hast a devil, in reply about his glory he says only this: I honor the Father, ascribing all to him, and I seek not my own glory as men do, who repay something for insults inflicted, but I reserve it for the Father, and there is one who seeketh and judgeth. There are two temptations. One of proving, of which: The Lord your God trieth you Deut. 13. The other of deceiving, of which: God is not a tempter of evils James 1. So also two fears: one which charity casteth out, the other which endureth for ever and ever. So also two judgments: one of condemnation, in which the Father does not judge, but hath given all judgment to the Son: the other of discernment; whence: Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause Psal. 42. According to this it is said: There is one that seeketh my glory and discerneth it from your glory, because you glory according to the world, I do not, but with that glory which I had with the Father before the world was, which is distinct from human puffing up.
8.51: 8.51 Amen, amen I say to you. Not I, but the Father seeketh my glory; and I say, If you say, Thou hast a devil, I call you to life. From this let the man Jesus teach us to render not evil but good. He shall not see. What is said, he shall see or taste, is nothing other than he shall experience.
8.52: 8.52 Now we know. As the good man, on receiving an insult, becomes better, so the wicked man becomes worse from a benefit.
8.53: 8.53 Whom dost thou make thyself? According to them he made himself the Son of God, equal to himself, as though he were not, but he did not make himself so, indeed he truly was; whence the Apostle: He thought it not robbery to be equal to God Phil. 2. Therefore not 'who art thou', but 'whom dost thou make thyself'?
8.54: 8.54 Jesus answered. Against what they say, 'Whom dost thou make thyself?', he refers his glory to the Father, from whom it is that he is God.
8.55: 8.55 It is my Father. He openly says that his Father is the God who was announced to the Jews: I do not announce to you a new God, but him in whose knowledge you are accustomed to glory. That glorifieth. The voice of the Father glorifies the Son at the baptism, on the mountain, and in other such instances. And you have not known him. You have not known him spiritually, while you served earthly things. Behold, he sees openly that they resist him, yet he does not cease to preach himself to them. And if I shall say, etc. Lest he seem to glory arrogantly in this, he adds, and if I shall say. Arrogance is to be avoided in such a way that the truth is not abandoned.
8.56: 8.56 Abraham. Believing, he rejoiced in hope that he might see by understanding so great a mystery. My day. AUG. It is uncertain whether it is the temporal day, etc., up to and that it itself was made flesh?
8.59: 8.59 And he went out. Going out of the temple, that is, from the figures of the Jews, let us see what he did in the temple of the Gentiles.
9.1: 9.1 And passing by. Not standing in the way of sinners, but alongside the way of our mortality. A man blind. The blind man signifies the human race, in which there is natural blindness, because when the first man sinned, the defect grew into nature, whence according to the mind every man is born blind.
9.3: 9.3 Neither hath this man sinned. They did sin indeed, but it was not by that sin that he was made to be born blind, but this is the cause, that the works of God should be made manifest in him. That by enlightening him, and by signifying through him what he would do in the blindness of the human race, the Son of God might be made manifest; whence he adds: I must work.
9.5: 9.5 As long as I am in the world. Not only then was Christ the light in the world, but always until the consummation of the world he is by faith with the elect, and it is the time of working. That night is the night of hell, in which it is lawful for no one to work, as it was not lawful for the burning rich man, but it is only the time of receiving.
9.6: 9.6 And made clay. As he formed the first man from the slime of the earth, so by the same kind of clay he reformed the human race. He made clay of spittle, because the Word was made flesh. The spittle is the wisdom which came forth from the mouth of the Most High. The earth is the flesh of Christ. He anointed his eyes. That is, he made him a catechumen, who believes the Word made flesh. Anointed, he does not yet see, but is sent to wash, that is, to be baptized in the One Sent, that is, in Christ, on account of which the name of the pool is interpreted. Baptized, he received light from sins.
9.7: 9.7 And he came seeing, etc. The question is asked how he healed this man without faith, when we read that he healed no one outwardly without inward healing. But this is said of those who were sick on account of sins: this man was afflicted not on account of sin but for the glory of God.
9.16: 9.16 This man is not of God, etc. He keeps the sabbath spiritually who is without sin; those do not who are servants of sin.
9.17: 9.17 What sayest thou, etc. They seek a pretext of calumny, that he might be driven from the synagogue, but be found by Christ. But he said, etc. Still anointed in heart, he confesses, yet does not lie.
9.18: 9.18 Till they called, etc. Mystically: The parents, that is, the devil or the vices, who say: He is of age, let him speak for himself, who do not want a man to confess Christ. Give glory to God: We know, etc. To give glory to God is to speak the truth about someone as though in the presence of God, that is: Confess that this man is not God as we are, but a sinner.
9.27: 9.27 Why would you hear it again, etc. AUG. Having been made seeing from blind, he is angry against their hardness, and no longer bearing the blind.
9.28: 9.28 They reviled him therefore. Their curse is according to their heart. But what is said is desirable for all, that they be disciples of Christ.
9.29: 9.29 But as for this man, we know not. Above they had said: We know this man; whence here they say they do not know; but we say we do not know the things we reject. He is not known, lies hidden in humility, is betrayed by the power of signs: it is not known whence he is, and as God he enlightens the blind.
9.33: 9.33 Unless this man were of God, etc. Their anger despised, he freely confesses the truth. For these things would not be done except by the Lord, nor by the disciples, unless God were in them.
9.34: 9.34 Thou wast wholly born in sins. That is, with closed eyes, which they say is for the sins of the parents, but Christ heals the whole, outside the eyes, within he opens the heart. And dost thou teach us? And they cast him out. By questioning so often that they might learn, they had made him a master, but, ungrateful, they cast out the one teaching. But because he was expelled, he was made more a Christian.
9.36: 9.36 Who is he, etc. Still anointed, by these words he shows that for a long time he had had a heart prepared to believe, but had not known in whom he ought to believe.
9.37: 9.37 And thou hast seen. Now the Lord washes the face of the anointed one, now he enlightens the eyes of the heart, and he confesses not only the Son of man but also the Son of God.
9.39: 9.39 That they who see not. That is, those who think they see seek to see, and they who see, that is, who think they see, do not seek the physician; and this is the judgment, that is, the discernment which distinguishes the cause of the believers from the proud. For he will make the judgment of condemnation not now but at the end; whence: I judge not any man.
10.1: 10.1 Amen, amen I say to you. Because the Pharisees boasted that they saw, as they could if they were sheep of Christ, the Lord, against their arrogance, sets forth a similitude about his flock and about the door by which one enters the fold, showing that neither wisdom, nor observance of the law, nor good life avails anything except through him: without him they are nothing, in any Jew, or Gentile, or philosopher, or Pharisee who teach how to live happily, or heretic under the name of Christ: nor yet in Christ preaching, but all without him plunder and kill. By the door. That is, by me, as he explains afterward. This door is lowly: whoever wishes to enter by it must humble himself, lest, if he is upright, he strike against the low door. A thief. Because what is another's he calls his own, that is, he makes God's sheep his own. A robber, because what he has stolen he kills. But all who hold and teach the truth in Christ the shepherd are one shepherd.
10.2: 10.2 Is the shepherd of the sheep. Christ is properly the shepherd according to the office of feeding the sheep, as he himself explains afterward, who by himself the door enters the fold of the sheep. But because others are sharers with him in the pastoral office, what is said of him properly also fits them in their own way. The door is that by which one enters; Christ therefore is the shepherd through himself the door, and whoever is a shepherd under him enters through that same door into the hearts of the sheep; because if he preaches something else, the sheep do not hear; if Christ, the sheep of Christ recognize this voice.
10.3: 10.3 To him the porter openeth. The porter, that is, Christ who opens himself, or the Scripture which leads to Christ, or the Holy Spirit who teaches all truth. And the sheep, etc. AUG. Some are true sheep, because the Lord knows, etc., up to this no one of his own despises, no stranger hears.
10.6: 10.6 But they understood not. The predestined sheep for a time do not know themselves, nor hear the voice of the shepherd, but at the end they persevere; on the contrary the wolves for a time hear, but at the end persevere.
10.8: 10.8 All, etc. A thief is one who enters through simony or in some other way against Christ, and after he has entered kills by bad example and so is openly a robber. Nor is such a one to be called a hireling, because when the wolf comes he does not resist, but yields for the wage. If, when the wolf violently drags off, he does not resist, he receives this wage, that he is not dragged away with the sheep, but afterward by living badly corrupts the sheep, and now, fallen back into another part, he becomes a thief or robber, losing the name of hireling.
10.9: 10.9 If any man. Here he shows evidently that not only the shepherd but the sheep too enter by the door. And shall go in. Within by thinking well, he shall go out outside by working well for the example of others. Or he shall go in to the Church, that here he may live by faith. Whence afterward he says: That they may have life. And he shall go out of this life, that he may live for ever. Whence afterward and may have it more abundantly; and shall find pastures, going in and going out.
10.10: 10.10 But to steal, etc. He steals by usurping another's property for himself, he kills by drawing away from the faith, he destroys unto eternal damnation.
10.12: 10.12 But the hireling, etc. The hireling is one who seeks his own things, not those of Christ, who serves God not for God's sake but for some wage; he is culpable, and is not a son, yet is necessary and to be tolerated. The thief, however, is always to be guarded against. Superiors who are sons are also shepherds, and yet there is one shepherd, because they are all members of him whose own the sheep are. And the wolf catcheth. The wolf is either the violent man who ravages bodily, or the devil who scatters spiritually, whom he who seeks not the souls of the sheep but his own things does not meet by resisting or by rebuking evils, which is to flee, because fear is the flight of the mind: he flees lest he lose what he loves, whence, giving the reason for the flight, he adds: Because he is a hireling and has no care for the sheep, but for his own things: shepherds, however, are not said to flee if they yield to persecution and preserve themselves for the usefulness of the sheep, to whom, though absent in body, they are present in spirit.
10.14: 10.14 I am the good shepherd. After the fault of the false one, he again sets forth the form of the true shepherd. I am the good shepherd and I lay down my life for my sheep. Which he did not do alone, except that all his own and he himself are one, because he could do this without them, they not without him, without whom they can do nothing.
10.15: 10.15 And I. The Son knows the Father by himself, we through him, as elsewhere: No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him Matth. 11. Likewise no one knoweth the Son but the Father, neither doth any one know the Father but the Son, and he to whom it shall please the Son to reveal him Matth. 11; Luke 10. And I lay down my life. This is the proof of love toward the Father and toward the sheep. So Peter also, confessing love a third time, is bidden to feed the sheep and to die for them. For the sheep. For the sheep of the house of Israel that were lost, to whom he was sent bodily, from whom those that are of the Gentiles are not unlike, whence he says:
10.16: 10.16 I must. Although through his own, because he is in them. And my voice. He does not say 'of mine', because he speaks in them.
10.17: 10.17 Therefore, etc. AUG. The Word from the time he took on man, that is, flesh and soul, etc., up to not by his own power, but by the power of the Deity inhabiting the flesh, namely.
10.22: 10.22 And it was the feast of the dedication, etc. Cænon means new. Hence encænia, that is, to initiate. Encænia, the feast of the dedication of the temple, which was made by Judas Machabeus in winter time. Winter is mentioned here to signify the cold Jews, who do not approach the fire, that is, do not believe in Christ. Solomon, however, after the temple was built, dedicated it in autumn III Kings 8. Zorobabel and Jesus the priest, after the captivity, dedicated the rebuilt temple in spring II Esdras 6. Judas Machabeus, on account of the profanation by Antiochus, in winter I Mach. 4.
10.23: 10.23 In the porch. The porches by which the temple was surrounded are usually signified by the name of the temple.
10.24: 10.24 The Jews therefore came round about him. While the Lord patiently preached the truth amid reproaches, they, blinded, do not obey, but tempt: How long dost thou hold our souls in suspense? They slander him as taking away souls who saves them, whom they thought a mere man, but one who would reign above all. If thou be the Christ, tell us plainly. They do not desire the truth, but prepare a calumny, that if he should say he is a king, they might hand him over to the authority as acting against Augustus. But the Lord so tempers his answer that there is no room for calumny for them, and that it may appear manifestly to the faithful, for whose sake these things are related, that he is the Christ, not man only, as they suppose, but the Son of God.
10.29: 10.29 And no man can snatch them out of the hand of my Father. Because from this, that I am of the Father, I am greater to protect than they to assail.
10.30: 10.30 I and the Father are one. By these words he not only resolves the question of the Jews, who came to tempt him, but also condemns the madness of future heretics.
10.31: 10.31 The Jews then took up stones. Those who had borne the rest no longer bear this, but, hard, run to stones. But because Jesus suffers only what he wills, he still speaks.
10.33: 10.33 Makest thyself. They understood that I and the Father are one could not be said except where there is equality of the Father and the Son, which Arius did not understand; but Christ, because he saw that they were slow and could not bear the splendor of the truth, tempered it in these words: Is it not written, etc.
10.34: 10.34 That I. God is spoken of in three ways: by nature, by adoption, as I said: You are gods; falsely, as demons and idols.
10.35: 10.35 If he called them gods. If men become gods by participating in the word of God, how is he who by nature is the Son, in whom they participate, not God?
10.38: 10.38 Believe the works. Give faith to the works, that by the merit of faith, knowing the works more fully, you may come to faith in the deity.
10.39: 10.39 That the Father is in me. The Father is in the Son, the Son in the Father, as equal in him to whom he is equal; whence he can also say: I and the Father are one. And he that seeth me seeth the Father also; and this is proper to him. But it is a gift to man by participation that he is said to be in God containing him and God in him, as in a vessel.
10.41: 10.41 And many came. These lay hold of him as one who remains, not as the wicked wished to lay hold of him as he departed. For John, etc. He did no sign in Jerusalem as this man, and whatever he said he bore testimony to him, as if through a lamp we come to the day.
11.1: 11.1 Now there was a certain man sick. While he stays beyond the Jordan, Lazarus falls sick, and the sisters send to him there. These sisters of Lazarus are a figure of the Jews already received into eternal blessedness, who for the healing of their brother, that is, for the rest still wandering in the darkness of ignorance, supplicate the Lord by a very well-known action. Lazarus sick. Lazarus is a figure of the Jews who were weak in the faith of Christ: Martha and Mary signify the teaching of the good Jews.
11.3: 11.3 Behold, he whom thou lovest, etc. Lazarus, by whom the sinner is signified, who is loved by the Lord, because he came not to call the just but sinners. The sisters are the good thoughts of the sinner, which pray for the loosing of sins.
11.4: 11.4 For the glory of God, etc. That is, that the Son of God may be glorified. Behold, he calls himself God, against those who say that the Son of God is not God.
11.5: 11.5 Loved. The Savior of the sick and raiser of the dead loved Lazarus, because sick and dead.
11.6: 11.6 Two days. That four days might be completed. For on the first day, on which it was announced to him, the sick man died beyond the Jordan; he stayed two days, behold three; on the fourth day he came.
11.7: 11.7 Let us go into Judea. Mystically: It signifies faith about to return to the Jews at the end through Elias and Enoch.
11.8: 11.8 The disciples say to him. Frightened, wishing to give counsel to the master that he not die, as elsewhere Peter: Lord, be it far from thee, this shall not be unto thee. But as Peter is praised for what is another's: Blessed art thou, Simon Bar-Jona, because the Father revealed it to thee, he is blamed for what is his own. Go behind me, Satan, because thou savourest not the things that are of God, but that are of men. So he rebuked these also, saying he is the day in which they ought to walk lest they stumble, and walking without him they stumble, since they now are unwilling that he should die who came to die for men. He says they are the hours that follow the day, not that they are days, but the day illumines them. Twelve is a sacred number which remains full: for when Judas, who did not shine among the hours, was cast down, another was substituted.
11.9: 11.9 Are there not twelve hours. HIER. Christ is the day, and otherwise the apostles are the day; how Christ, etc., up to the twelve apostles themselves are understood.
11.15: 11.15 That you may believe. Not that they would now begin to believe, but that they might believe more firmly. For their faith was always increased by miracles.
11.17: 11.17 And found. AUG. Mystically: There are four days of death. Man is born, etc., up to but mercy does not leave even such.
11.22: 11.22 But now also I know. This I know, that thou canst raise him if thou wilt, which I leave to thy judgment, but I do not presume, nor do I ask that thou raise him, since I do not know whether a resurrection would be useful.
11.25: 11.25 Although he be dead. Jesus raised three dead: one in the house, that is, in the heart; the second at the gate, that is, in the mouth; the third in the tomb, that is, in the work and habit of sinning. Shall live. As Abraham, Isaac and Jacob live, of whom God is called God as of the living. The believer, even dead, lives, as the unbeliever, even living, is dead.
11.28: 11.28 Secretly. Because if the Jews had heard that she was called by Jesus, they would not have followed, and so would not have seen the miracle. But because they supposed that they were going to the sepulchre of their brother, they followed. And calleth for thee. For brevity's sake, in the words of Martha he shows something not said before, namely that the Lord had called Mary.
11.31: 11.31 They followed her. The evangelist took care to narrate these things so that we may see what occasion caused the resurrection of a man four days dead to have more witnesses.
11.33: 11.33 He groaned in the spirit. Note the power: He himself groaned and troubled himself, whom no other could trouble, as he took on all things of this kind, because he willed. It signifies, however, how much man ought to be troubled, pressed by so great a mass of sin. When the sinner, reckoning what good things of God he has received, what evils he has returned, groans in spirit and is troubled: Christ groans in him and is troubled, because faith in Christ is Christ in the heart. Faith groans in man when it rebukes him for his sins.
11.34: 11.34 Where have you laid him? He who knew absent that he was dead knows also where he is buried, but by speaking so he signifies that he as it were does not know the lost man; whence it is said: I know you not Matth. 7. And: Where art thou, Adam? Gen. 3.
11.38: 11.38 Jesus therefore, etc. He shows the difficulty of giving life to such a sinner. Now it was a cave. Morally: Every sinner, pressed by the mass of sins and weighed down by his law and, now stinking by his evil habit, openly corrupts others by his bad example: the sisters are certain thoughts, because when at times he thinks he has done ill, he grieves.
11.39: 11.39 Lord, by this time he stinketh. She feared that, the stone removed, a stench would be raised rather than her brother raised up.
11.42: 11.42 But because of the people, etc. By these words he shows that he seeks the glory of the Father, as in his other works. For because according to the man he was less than the Father, he asks of him the raising of Lazarus, and therefore says he was heard, and this because of the bystanders, that thus they might believe him the Son of God.
11.43: 11.43 With a loud voice. He groaned, wept, cried out, because he rises with difficulty whom the mass of an evil habit presses down, yet nevertheless after a loud voice he rises, that is, by the great grace of God he is given life while he repents.
11.44: 11.44 And presently he came forth. While the sinner despises, he lies buried; when he repents, he rises; when he confesses, he comes forth, as it were manifest from coming out of hidden places. Loose him. Christ by himself gives life within, to the ministers he gives the power of loosing.
11.48: 11.48 They will believe in him. And the Romans will come. And because they felt that his doctrine was against the temple and the laws of the fathers, they feared lest, if all believed in Christ, no one would remain to defend the city of God and the temple against the Romans. And the Romans will come. They fear for temporal things, not for eternal, and they lost both. The place is Jerusalem, which they lost; they lost their nation, dispersed everywhere.
11.51: 11.51 This he spoke not of himself. AUG. Note that even the wicked foretell future things by the spirit of prophecy, etc., up to which is not lawful except for the high priest, as is read of Zacharias.
11.52: 11.52 For the nation. Of the Jews, namely, among whom were sheep, this only Caiphas said. But because the evangelist knew there were other sheep, he added: But that he might gather together in one the children of God that were dispersed. Children by predestination, as also the sheep in Israel, for they were not yet, because they had not yet believed.
11.55: 11.55 Now the Pasch was at hand. With the figurative Pasch imminent, in which the true Lamb is now to be immolated, there was counsel among the Jews about killing him, and he himself draws near to the place of his passion.
12.1: 12.1 He came to Bethania. He came to Bethania first so that the raising of Lazarus might be committed more deeply to the memory of all, and the Jews, inexcusable, be confounded, in treating of the death of so great a raiser.
12.3: 12.3 Mary therefore. Precious ointment is made of nard, chiefly from the spikes; here, however, it is called spikenard from the place it was from. And it is interpreted faithful, not corrupted by any admixture. Then one of his disciples said. Judas, though wicked, is nevertheless numbered among the apostles, that we may be taught to tolerate the wicked, lest we divide the body of Christ, and that the wicked do not harm the good.
12.6: 12.6 Not because, etc. As to his intention, the poor did not concern him, because he did not care for them, not because it had been committed to him to dispense to the poor. Having the purse, etc. He whom angels serve has a purse for the expenses of the poor, condescending to the weak.
12.7: 12.7 Let her alone. He knows the thief, but does not betray him, teaching to tolerate the wicked. He commends so great a service of Mary, showing that he was about to die and to be anointed with spices for burial. Therefore to Mary, to whom it was not permitted to anoint the dead, it was given to honor the living with the duty of the funeral, whence according to Mark it is said, what she had, that is, what she could, she did; she is come beforehand to anoint my body for burial.
12.8: 12.8 But me you have not always. By bodily presence. Or you will not have, you Judas and those like you, because if the wicked now communicate in the sacraments, yet afterward they do not have the Lord as the good do.
12.9: 12.9 And they came. Curiosity, not charity, brought these. We, on the contrary, if we know that Jesus has found the house of an obedient soul in which to dwell, let us come there in contemplation, not only on account of the man whom we see raised up in the soul, but that we may imitate the good life, and through this come to the vision of Jesus.
12.10: 12.10 But the chief priests thought. Because they could not hide or deny the miracle, they foolishly wish to kill, as though he who raised one dead could not raise one killed.
12.12: 12.12 On the next day. Behold, the sheep from Israel come to the shepherd. The branches are praises signifying the victory of him who is going to overcome the devil and death.
12.13: 12.13 Cried. AUG. Hosanna is the voice of one beseeching, showing an affection more than signifying any thing, like interjections. King of Israel. A king not in the earthly manner, which is little, but because he rules, and leads both to minds and to the kingdoms of heaven, and it is of mercy, not of indignation.
12.15: 12.15 Fear not, daughter. In the reprobate people there was a daughter of Sion, that is, of Jerusalem, namely the sheep who devoutly run to meet him as he comes, to whom it is said divinely: Recognize him whom you praise, and fear not when he suffers who is your redemption. The colt on which no man yet sat is the people of the Gentiles, which had not received the law of God.
12.19: 12.19 Behold, the whole. Through his passion and resurrection he redeemed the whole world, and it followed him. And what wonder if the world goes after him through whom the world was made?
12.21: 12.21 These therefore came. He shows the Gentiles converted through the preaching of the apostles.
12.23: 12.23 And Jesus. They were of the Jews who cried: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; now the Gentiles seek to see, behold two walls meeting. So the cornerstone speaks. The hour is come that the Son of man should be glorified. This is not the glorification of these who wish to see, but on the occasion of these he announces the coming fullness of the Gentiles when he is glorified in the heavens. But the humility of the passion precedes this height of glorification, whence: Amen, amen I say to you, etc. Where he says he is a grain to be mortified and multiplied, to which passion, having now exhorted, he adds: He that loveth his life, etc. Unless the grain of wheat. AUG. He himself is the wheat by which the faithful soul ought to live. The grain, from which the spiritual harvest ought to arise. Although there are many grains of seeds, he compares himself to none but wheat, whence the custom began in the Church that the body of the Lord be made of this grain alone.
12.25: 12.25 He that loveth. AUG. He who loves in this life loses in the future what is more fitting, whence he adds: He that hateth his life, etc. He does not love but hates his life in this world who, loving God, chooses rather to be killed than to sin against him.
12.26: 12.26 If any man minister to me. The reward of the work by which he is served is to be with him, without whom it is nowhere well to be, and with whom it is nowhere ill to be, whence he adds more openly, if any man minister to me.
12.27: 12.27 Now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? The passion foretold and the exhortation to it added, as though having given the voice of his strength, he adds the feeling of our weakness, which he truly took on, but willingly for us, lest we despair of this weakness: in which he also teaches what we ought to say, and where to take refuge. As if to say: My soul is troubled, what shall I say? whither shall I flee? whom shall I call upon? in whom shall I hope? In the Father who saves, to whom I set forth my will, because for this reason I came to this hour, that I might suffer these things, whence the glorification is thus made to me and in my members.
12.28: 12.28 Father, glorify. I seek salvation, but I do not refuse the passion, on account of which passion glorify me, which is the glory of thy name.
12.30: 12.30 This voice came not because of me. He shows that this voice did not indicate to him what he knew, but to those to whom it ought to be indicated.
12.31: 12.31 Now is the judgment. Of discernment, namely, which is before the last judgment of condemnation, because now, the right of the devil destroyed by the passion, many will be freed, whence in explaining he adds: I suffer, I am troubled, and through these, etc. Shall be cast out. He will be expelled from the redeemed; he will be fully expelled by the preaching apostles, he who once, though tempting from outside, did not harm within, to a few.
12.34: 12.34 And how sayest thou, etc. How will he die on the cross? For they thought he had said this because they were planning to do it. The Son of man. Because they remembered this, that he had often said he was the Son of man, not that he had said here, if the Son of man be lifted up. Who is this Son of man? For if he is the Christ, he abideth for ever. If he abideth for ever, how shall he be lifted up from the earth, that is, die on the cross?
12.35: 12.35 Walk. That is, understand the whole, and that Christ is to die that he may redeem one who will live for ever in heaven, whither he leads him. Or while you have Christ with you, lest the darkness of ignorance and perpetual death overtake you. Knoweth not whither he goeth. He who does not believe the death of Christ knows not whither he goes, but stumbles on the rock of scandal, which is Christ, the Jews despising and deriding him dead.
12.36: 12.36 While you have the light. That is, while you understand something true of the eternity of Christ, believe in the truth by adding concerning his humility, that you may be born again in the truth. From them. Not from those who had begun to believe, but from those who envied. That he hid himself, he took counsel for our infirmity, he did not detract from his own power.
12.38: 12.38 That the saying of Isaias might be fulfilled. Which it is necessary to be fulfilled in all ways, yet not to be done by necessity but by will, for God foreknew and foretold that they would not believe and would sin, yet he did not compel them to this, but as it happens he so foreknew and foretold.
12.39: 12.39 They could not. AUG. Not that men cannot be changed for the better, but as long as they are such they cannot believe.
12.43: 12.43 The glory of God. Therefore the cross is fixed on the forehead of believers, where is the seat of shame, that no one may blush at the name of Christ, and may seek the glory of God rather than that of men.
12.44: 12.44 Jesus. Some not believing, others believing, either openly with palms and praises or in secret, his passion already drawing near, Jesus cries out, who lay hidden as long as the passion was not to be completed. He that believeth in me. Because he appeared as man, and God lay hidden in the man, lest they think him to be only what they saw, he wishes himself to be believed such and so great as the Father is.
12.45: 12.45 And he that seeth me seeth him also that, etc. So far is there nothing between me and him that he who sees me sees him. This vision is not carnal but intellectual, in the clean of heart. He that seeth me. He does not say 'does not see me', but 'him that sent me', as he said, he that believeth in me, believeth not in me, but in him that sent me, because he said that lest he be believed only as he appeared, the Son of man; but he said this that he might be believed equal to the Father. Neither of these would another sent, that is, an apostle, say, because he is only a servant. But he can say other things in common with the Son, as he who heareth or receiveth me heareth and receiveth him that sent me, because the Lord is honored in the servant and the Father in the Son.
12.46: 12.46 I am the light. Of no other is it said: The light is come into the world, except of him who enlightens; the rest, as enlightened, are light because their life shines for men. The word that I have spoken. He says manifestly that he will judge on the last day, because he is the word of the Father who spoke himself, announced himself.
12.49: 12.49 Commandment. The Father did not give the Son a commandment through an angel or other creature. Nor a commandment which he had at some time not known: but when he begot the Word and wisdom in which are all commandments, he gave it: as to the Son who is life, by that he gave him life by which he begot life, because by begetting he gave life to be, which was without defect.
12.50: 12.50 And I know. Since he says the commandment is life everlasting, and he himself is life everlasting, he openly says that he is the commandment of God. The things therefore that I speak, as the Father said to me, so I speak. To understanding minds, as the truth is born of the Father, but thus the truth speaks within without sound, as the Father said to him; that men might believe what they cannot yet understand, words sounded from the mouth of flesh, which, uttered and marked in letters, raise us in some measure to the truth itself.
13.1: 13.1 That he should pass. The evangelist interprets for us the name of the pasch, that is, passage, and its signification, that as they from Egypt, so Christ from the world. So also we, marked with the blood of the Lamb, from vices to virtues, from the world to heaven. He loved them unto the end. Unto the end, that is, unto Christ who is the consummating end, that is, that by love of him they may pass whither he himself passes. Or unto the end, that is, unto death, not that his love is terminated by death, but he so loved that love led him as far as death, in which he gave an example that all may remain in God's truth to the end.
13.2: 13.2 And supper being ended. The supper signifies the passion. For as after supper there is no dinner, so Christ, after he has suffered once, does not suffer again. He riseth from supper, after the passion lays aside his garments, according to the former weakness he girded himself with a towel, with the same flesh now immortal, he putteth water into a basin, that is, the grace of baptism, he washeth the feet and wipeth them from sins in baptism, he took his garments, that is, the Jews at the end of the world, whom he had first laid aside, blinded.
13.4: 13.4 He riseth from supper. From that heavenly refection with which he was refreshed with the angels, he layeth aside his garments, the glory of eternal blessedness. And layeth aside his garments. He passed over the height, to set beneath it his humility, so that humility might be perfectly commended to man when one so high had so humbled himself as to wash even the feet of the traitor.
13.5: 13.5 After that, he putteth. He shed his blood on the earth to cleanse the footsteps of believers, which were foul with earthly sins.
13.8: 13.8 Peter saith to him, etc. Because of the height of the promised mystery he does not yet permit it to be done, not yet able to bear that God be humbled to his feet, terrified with awe. He answered. He who is not washed by baptism and confession of penance has no part with Jesus.
13.9: 13.9 Simon Peter saith to him. Peter's error here profited us. For he erred that we might not err. He erred when he offered himself to God to be washed all over, and God corrected him, showing that one once baptized is not to be baptized again.
13.10: 13.10 He that is washed. From these words we understand that the apostles were baptized, though we do not read where or when. He that is washed. He who is washed by baptism is clean.
