But because he is again defiled by the dust of the earthly dwelling, there is again need to wash the feet, which the Lord washes interceding for us, and we ourselves by praying. He also who in leisure studies the truth, while he goes on to open to the bridegroom knocking in the case of others, defiles his feet, because the truth is humbly heard but cannot be preached without danger, but these feet the Lord washes for the disciples.
13.12: 13.12 And when he was set down again, he said to them: Know you what I have done to you? You call me, etc. As before by example, so now also by word the master of truth instructs them. And that he says great things of himself is not arrogance but truth, which profits the hearers, as Paul also does. GREG. The humble are incautious who ensnare themselves with a lie while they avoid arrogance, because they raise themselves against the truth, which they leave. For he who, under compulsion of necessity, says true and good things of himself, is so much the more joined to humility as he is allied to truth.
13.18: 13.18 I speak not of you all. You will not all do this by which you may be blessed, but he that eateth my bread, not that he may profit but that he may lie hid, will lift up his heel against me, that is, will trample on me, that the Scripture may be fulfilled which foretold this, not that it compels, but because it did not keep silent about what was to be.
13.19: 13.19 At present I tell you. As if to say: Until now I have borne and been silent, but now I point out the traitor before it happens, which is soon to be done, that when it is done you may believe that I am he of whom that Scripture foretold.
13.20: 13.20 Amen, amen I say to you. After he taught them by his own example humiliation and the passion of the heel, he adds an honor with which to console them, that he and the Father are received in them.
13.21: 13.21 When Jesus had said these things. Our infirmity was truly troubled in him, not his power, as he also truly suffered. He willingly took on the trouble, lest the servant, troubled by necessity, despair. That he is troubled signifies that the spiritual, out of charity, are to be troubled when an urgent cause forces them to separate even the cockle from the wheat before the harvest.
13.26: 13.26 And when he had dipped the bread. The dipping of the bread signifies the pretense of Judas, who came to the supper as a feigned friend. For things which are dipped are not cleansed but stained. But if the dipping signifies something good, damnation followed not undeservedly for one ungrateful to that same good. He gave it to Judas Simon's son Iscariot, etc. Not, as some think, did Judas now receive the body of Christ. For it must be known that the Lord had already distributed the sacrament of the body and blood to all, among whom Judas also was, then by the dipped morsel the traitor himself is indicated, etc.
13.27: 13.27 That which thou dost. He does not command, but foretells evil to Judas, good to us, because he wishes this to be done quickly, not so much hastening to his punishment as to the salvation of the faithful.
13.29: 13.29 Because he had the purse. In which the offerings were collected for the needs of his own and of others in want. In this is given a form for the Church of keeping necessary things, which is commanded not to think of tomorrow, lest it serve for earthly things, or through fear of want desert justice.
13.30: 13.30 And it was night. The night suits the sacrament. For he who went out was a son of darkness doing the works of darkness. Now is the Son of man glorified. AUG. When Judas went out, for whom it was said: You are not all clean, etc., up to as though it were done which soon is to be.
13.33: 13.33 Little children. ID. Because he had said that God would quickly glorify him, etc., up to this cannot be taken so; because what follows would not fit. Whither I go you cannot come. The apostles, not yet strengthened by the Spirit, could not now follow the Lord, that is, die for the Lord and for justice, or come to the immortal life to which he himself was going, but they were to follow afterward. How, however, they can be fit and go whither he goes before, he teaches. A new commandment I give. AUG. Not that this is not in the old law, Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself, etc., up to which love makes one die to the world.
13.34: 13.34 That you love one another as I have loved you. Let this not be thought to omit the love of God which is in the love of neighbor, for in the neighbor only God is loved, as Christ also in us loves God, and not that we may have this, but that we might have it, as a physician in the sick man loves not the disease but the health which he came to give.
13.36: 13.36 Lord, whither, etc. Having heard, whither I go, and having understood the way by which he can follow, that is, love, Peter speaks as one ready to follow. And because the Lord knew this his mind, he said he could not now, in which he did not take away the hope of the future, but confirmed it. But thou shalt follow afterwards.
13.37: 13.37 My life. He presumes much who promises to lay down his life for him who has not yet given his life for Peter, as though he could go first. AUG. Knowing his will but not his strength, like the weak man he boasts his will, but the physician was looking at the weakness. The one promised, the other foreknew, and he who did not know was hearing, he who foreknew was teaching.
13.38: 13.38 The cock shall not crow, etc. Peter begins the threefold denial before the first crowing of the cock, but completes it all before the second crowing of the cock.
14.1: 14.1 Let not your heart be troubled, etc. AUG. So that they might not fear death as if it were merely a man's, and so be troubled, etc., up to: one is the brightness of the moon, another the brightness of the stars.
14.2: 14.2 In my Father's house, etc. The house of God, the temple of God, the kingdom of God. The kingdom of heaven is the just, among whom there are many differences. And these are the mansions of that house. AUG. For now the just are the kingdom of God and the kingdom of heaven, etc., up to: what you are in hope, you may be in reality. If not, etc. That is, if I had not predestined a mansion (which is unfitting with respect to God, who predestined all good things before all times), then I would now be preparing, that is, predestining, which again is unfitting, with respect to God, to predestine something in the present. THE SAME. He confirms that they exist, for if they did not exist he would have said, I will go and prepare, etc., up to: and this is the multitude of mansions.
14.3: 14.3 And if I shall go. THE SAME. He went away by being hidden, he comes by appearing, but he remains by ruling, so that we may advance by living well, and thus the place is prepared. THE SAME. Faith, which does not see, believes, for if it saw, etc., up to: the longing of love is the preparation of the mansion.
14.4: 14.4 And whither I go. This was said in accord with some who knew both the Son and the Father. Thomas, though he thought he did not know, is convinced by the very fact that he knew him, and knew the way and the life, that is, the Son and the Father. Of these who know it is added: From henceforth you shall know him, known through me, and you have seen him in your heart, since you have seen me in all things like him.
14.5: 14.5 Thomas saith to him, etc. He who does not lie said that they knew where and by what way one goes, but Thomas says that they know neither, not knowing that they know; but Christ convinces them that they know, because if they knew him, and he himself is the way, they knew the way, and if they knew him, and he himself is the truth and the life, then they knew the truth and the life to which he goes: he himself therefore goes by himself as the way, to himself as the truth and the life, and to the Father, because he is one with the Father.
14.7: 14.7 If you had known me. Since he had said that no one comes to the Father but by himself, who is inseparably the same as the Father, lest they should ask who the Father is, he shows that the Father is known from himself who is known, which some had not yet recognized, and he rebukes them, saying: If you had known me, etc. And you have seen him. As is said of two persons altogether alike: If you have seen this one, you have seen that one; they had therefore seen the Son who was most like the Father, but they had to be admonished to understand the Father also as such, and not unlike him.
14.9: 14.9 How sayest thou. And since he is altogether like. How sayest thou, etc. As if he were saying: I see in what spirit you speak; you do not seek another like him, but you think a better one. From myself. Because I who speak am not from myself: he attributes what he does to him from whom he himself, who does it, is.
14.12: 14.12 He that believeth in me. I and the Father work without difference. And whosoever believeth in me (lest this be taken as of the apostles alone) the works that I do through myself, he also shall do, that is, I do in him or through him, and greater than these. The works that I do. Yet not from himself, but from me. The servant is not greater than his lord. For he himself does many things without them, while they can do nothing without him except sin. Greater than these. AUG. Because while he himself healed by the hem of his garment, Peter healed by his shadow. Or his work, etc., up to: because if both are of equal power, this is of greater mercy.
14.15: 14.15 If you love me. How does he urge them to love and keep the commandments so that they may receive the Spirit, when unless they have him they cannot love and keep them? But what they had less openly, they were to receive more manifestly, so that what they had would become known to them.
14.16: 14.16 And I will ask the Father. THEOPH. I will ask, that is, I will beseech the Father, and he shall send you another Paraclete, etc., up to: that the Spirit the Paraclete may altogether come upon them, and his grace, condescending to them, he says to them: I will ask the Father.
14.17: 14.17 Because it seeth him not, etc. Lovers of the world do not have the spiritual eyes with which to see the Holy Spirit. Nor indeed can they see him with bodily eyes, because the Holy Spirit did not appear clothed in humanity. And shall be in you. He will be in you, he will not merely remain so as to be, since to be somewhere comes before remaining. Let no one therefore think that he remains as a guest visibly with another, but he can be known in them, not by others.
14.18: 14.18 I will not leave you. The Spirit will not be given in my place in such a way that I am not also with you. Orphans in Greek, wards in Latin.
14.19: 14.19 Yet a little while and the world. But the world, which now sees with the eyes of the flesh, will not see after a little while, because having risen he did not show himself to them, but the whole time is a little while, at the end of which the wicked one will be taken away that he may not see the glory of God, which the just will see. Because I live, and you shall live. He uses the present because his resurrection is soon to be. He uses the future for those whose resurrection is at the end.
14.20: 14.20 And you in me, and I in you. This is so now, and is known in a way through faith; but then it will be known by sight, when this union, which is now begun, shall be perfected.
14.21: 14.21 He that hath, etc. Not only you apostles will live and know, but whoever has them in memory and keeps them in life. Or, he has them by doing, keeps them by persevering. Or, he who has them in words keeps them in conduct. Or, he has them by hearing, keeps them by doing. And I will love him. I will love him for this, that I may manifest; for he loves now also, but not for this, but rather that we may believe and keep the commandments, so that we may merit what we shall receive afterward. And I will manifest. He who has my commandment, he knows me, and this is what is meant by: I will manifest myself to him. But he first puts forward the cause of the commandment, that he loves me, and he who loves me, my Father will love him, and because the Father does, then I will love him, and from this comes the manifestation.
14.22: 14.22 Judas saith to him, etc. Having heard that the world will now see him but they themselves will see him, Judas, asking on behalf of all, inquires the cause of this distinction. And this cause, according to the Lord's answer, is love, by which alone and by no other thing the holy nation is distinguished from the unholy.
14.23: 14.23 We will come to him. God comes to man when man comes to God. Man comes by believing, obeying, contemplating, receiving; God comes by helping, enlightening, fulfilling. And will make our abode, etc. Charity causes one to dwell in the house in which the Father and the Son make their abode, whence he will also give the manifestation about which that man had inquired.
14.25: 14.25 These things have I spoken to you. These things concern the abiding in his lovers, in which the future spiritual Church is signified, in which the blessed are those from whom he does not depart. Abiding with you. Here is the present bodily Church, in which he visits by freeing, and returns.
14.26: 14.26 The Paraclete. Although to console is a work of the Trinity, yet it belongs chiefly to the person of the Holy Spirit, because in Scripture the Holy Spirit is designated by the name of goodness: through goodness, therefore, God consoles us, and through it he bestows on us all his good things. He will teach you. For although the Son teaches us and reveals the Father, he does all this through his goodness. He will teach you all things. He will teach what I shall have said; not that the Son says and the Spirit teaches, because what he says and teaches, the Trinity itself says and teaches. But since it is a Trinity, the individual persons must be indicated, whom we ought to hear distinctly and understand inseparably. When we say, therefore, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, we do not speak of them as together, since they cannot be other than together.
14.27: 14.27 Peace I leave with you. About to go to the Father. Peace, etc. And repeating the same: My peace I give unto you. And this is what the Prophet says: Peace upon peace Isa. 27.. There is peace in this world, abiding in which we conquer the enemy, love one another, and do not judge one another about hidden things. There will be peace in the future, when we shall reign without an enemy, where one will not be able to disagree with another, where all things are open and praise is given to each I Cor. 4.. But in him and from him are both peaces. For he is our peace Ephes. 2., and we believe him because he is, and we shall see him as he is. Hence what he says, my, is to be understood from the latter also of the former. Or the peace in this world is ours, which is some and not full, and from him in the future is his peace, where nothing resists, as he himself has it. Let not be troubled. Because I leave you in peace, let not your heart be troubled over what I said, I go, as if the wolf would attack at the absence of the shepherd, for as man I go, as God I am present.
14.28: 14.28 If you loved me. AUG. This was to go to him and to depart from us, etc., up to: that incorruptible dust might sit at the right hand of the Father. You would rejoice, etc. Because congratulation is due to human nature, which is raised to the right hand of the Father, in which the rest hope for the same for themselves. You may believe. Not because you have seen what was done, for there is no praise or merit of faith in that, nay, there is not even faith in what is seen, but in what is not seen. But that you may believe me to be the Son of God, not with a new faith, for they had believed even before, but with faith increased and renewed, because even now, when he said this, it was small, and when he died, none.
14.30: 14.30 And in me, etc. The Lord did not wish to have anything that he could lose; he came poor so that the devil would have nothing to take away.
15.1: 15.1 I am the true vine. You ought also to follow me as I go before you to the passion, because I am the vine, that is, your head, of the same nature as you, so that in me human nature may bear fruit. And my Father, etc. I too am a husbandman with the Father, because I am the pruner of the branches, which is the office of the husbandman, not of the vine, who also makes the branches workers, though not from his own and not through them, but through myself.
15.3: 15.3 Because of the word, etc. He does not say: because of the water of baptism, since even that without the word is only water; through the word it becomes a sacrament.
15.5: 15.5 I am, etc. He who thinks that he bears fruit from himself is not in the vine. Hence, with repetition and explanation of the above, he adds: I am the vine, you the branches. Clinging to me as to a vine. He that abideth in me. And therefore whoever (not only you) abides in me by believing, obeying, persevering. And I in him. By enlightening, helping, giving perseverance. He beareth. And although Christ is the vine according to his humanity, yet he would not give this grace to the branches unless he were also God.
15.6: 15.6 If any one. Cut-off branches are more worthless than all other wood, because they are assigned to no uses, but to the fire; either they are in the vine or in the fire.
15.7: 15.7 And my words. The words of God are then said to abide in us when we do what he commands and love what he promises. But he who does not do this touches, but does not cling, and so they are not to him for a benefit but for a testimony of condemnation. You shall ask. If a faithful person asks for something and it is not done, he is not asking for what the abiding in him has, nor what his words that are in him have, but what the desire and weakness of the flesh has.
15.8: 15.8 In this is my Father glorified, etc. He who abides in me bears much fruit, which is from the grace of God, and so the glory is his, not man's, and this is: In this, etc. That you bring forth very much fruit. As he shows not the equality of our nature and his own, but the grace by which he is Mediator, for the Father loves us, but in the Son. You shall be made. How? If you love me. From what love? From the observance of the commandments. If you love me as the Father hath loved me, not as much as. For equality is not indicated, but likeness, giving them eternal eternity.
15.11: 15.11 That joy. The joy of God over us, who foreknew and predestined, is always full; in us it begins from faith, grows, and indeed will be perfected in the resurrection.
15.12: 15.12 This is my commandment, etc. Above also concerning love of neighbor, but the repetition is a confirmation: there, however, he says: A commandment I give, as though it had not been before; here, however, This is, as though there were no other. There, New, lest we remain in oldness; here, My, lest it be despised.
15.13: 15.13 Greater than this. He defines the fullness of the mutual love which he commands them to have.
15.15: 15.15 I will not now call. Having commended love, he adds what belongs to condescension, that he calls good servants (who know by doing what he commands) friends, and takes from them the name of servant, which is cast out by fear, who does not know what his lord does. Because when he does something, he is so exalted as if he himself did it, not the lord.
15.17: 15.17 These things I command, etc. Here he shows what the fruit is which he had spoken of, for which the Father will also give what we ask, who has also given this, that we may love. That you love. AUG. He rightly commends love often, as though it alone were to be commanded, without which the rest cannot be, and which cannot be had without the rest. For the sake of it we ought to bear patiently even all the adversities of the world. Hence he adds:
15.18: 15.18 If the world. By the name of the world sometimes the good, sometimes the bad are designated, because it is one mass which all perished in Adam, from which some vessels are made unto honor, others unto dishonor.
15.19: 15.19 The world would love its own. If a wicked man punishes the crime of a wicked man, the world in part hates what is its own; while it punishes, in part it loves, because the wicked favors the wicked.
15.20: 15.20 My word. Namely this: There is not. And of that earlier one: Know ye that it hath hated me before you. And he adds the reason: The servant is not greater, etc. Because by his own example (than which there is no better) he admonished them to bear the hatred of the world, he adds why they ought to imitate him in this, because he is the Lord, they the servants.
15.22: 15.22 If I had not come. Here he shows more expressly the Jews, to whom he came, of whom he had spoken above under the name of the world. And because he came to them, here he shows them inexcusable for all their evils. Excuse, etc. Those to whom he did not come nor speak have an excuse, not for every sin, but for this, that they did not believe in Christ. But those to whom he came and spoke in the apostles are not excused. As for the former, who have sinned without the law, they shall perish without the law Rom. 2.. Of sin. That they do not believe me but hate me, and persecute me in myself and in mine, but this sin against me also redounds upon the Father, because he that hateth me, hateth my Father also. And what is gravest, not only did I come and speak, but I did works which, seeing, they hate both me and the Father.
15.24: 15.24 Which no other man, etc. AUG. That he fed so many thousands from a few loaves, that he went upon the waters, etc., up to: and because he did it himself through himself, none without him. They hated, etc. The Jews say that they love God, and yet they hate him without knowing it, because those who wish to be evil do not wish the truth to exist by which they are condemned. And as they hate their own punishment, they hate the truth which inflicts the punishment, not knowing that he is the truth. And if they hate the truth, they hate him from whom the truth was born, and so, not knowing the Father, they hate the truth born of him.
15.25: 15.25 They hated me. He hates without cause who seeks no advantage from hatred nor flees any disadvantage. So the wicked hate Christ. So the just love without cause, not for another reason but for himself.
15.26: 15.26 But when. Now, seeing the works, they hate both me and the Father without cause. But when the Paraclete is come, he will convict by a more manifest testimony those who saw and hated, and some of them, pricked by such a great crime, he will convert. Whom I will send. On the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit came upon a hundred and twenty persons assembled, with whom were all the apostles, in the house where the supper had been. Who proceedeth from the Father. The Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, but the Son is said to proceed from the Father because he is accustomed to refer to the Father, and what is his, from whom he himself is. From whom, therefore, he has his being, from him the Spirit has it that he proceeds from him.
16.1: 16.1 These things I have spoken, etc. After he taught by his own example to bear hatred, in which they know what they ought to do but are not able, after he also promised the Spirit by whom they will be able to resist, he adds: These things I have spoken, etc. This is an example regarding the Spirit who will strengthen, so that, charity being thus poured forth in your hearts, you may have much peace and no scandal.
16.2: 16.2 But the hour cometh. As if he were to say: If, driven out by them, you gain so many for me (at which you should rejoice), they will not be satisfied with driving you out. But they will not let you live, lest you gain them all, so that you turn them away from Judaism, in which they believe that the God of Israel and his holy things are being abandoned.
16.4: 16.4 But these things. After he told of their future sufferings and that the Spirit the consoler was to be given to them, he adds: These things I told you not, etc. If we take this as about the sufferings, he had foretold them not only after the supper but also before the approaching Pasch, and from the beginning of the mission of the twelve apostles; but he had not foretold the consolation of the Spirit that would come to them, because he himself was with them as advocate or consoler by bodily presence; but since he is now about to go, it was needful that he should say that the one would come who would strengthen them against those who cast them out and kill them.
16.5: 16.5 I go to him. So openly that no one asks what he discerns by bodily sight; they saw him ascending in a cloud, certain of the glory, they who earlier, when the passion had been foretold, had asked: Lord, whither goest thou?
16.7: 16.7 For if, etc. Not that, being placed on earth, he could not give, but that they were not fit to receive unless they ceased to know him according to the flesh. But if. When your minds are thus caught up to heavenly things, the Spirit will be present, together with the Father and the Son. For having been made spiritual from carnal, they were to have the Trinity more fully, as was promised.
16.8: 16.8 He will convince. Not that the Son does not convince, but that the Spirit will give them charity and drive out fear, so that they may have freedom to convince. AUG. He who does not believe in Christ is convicted of sin. He is convicted, etc., up to: lest they be judged with the prince of the world, whom they imitate, who is judged. And of justice. Not of his own, but of the justice of those who believe, the world is convicted, in comparison with whom it is condemned. Hence he does not say: The world shall not see me, but You shall not see me, you apostles. Against the unbelievers who say, How shall we believe what we do not see? It is true justice to believe what is not seen, so that those who saw the man believed God. And when by the ascension the form of man was withdrawn from sight, then was it fulfilled in every respect: The just man liveth by faith.
16.10: 16.10 And now, etc. That is, you will never see me such as now, that is, mortal and to be judged, but glorified as judge. And this is the justice of faith, of which the Apostle says: And if we have known Christ according to the flesh, but now we know him so no more II Cor. 5., and because the world does not wish to receive this from them, it is convicted.
16.11: 16.11 Of judgment. Because if they follow him as condemned, they are condemned with him, and lest they believe they will be spared, they are terrified by the punishment of that proud one.
16.13: 16.13 All truth, etc. He promises that the Spirit will do the whole, not that in this life the whole is accomplished. Of himself, etc. AUG. Because he is not from himself, since the Father alone, etc., up to: has always known, knows, and will know.
16.14: 16.14 He shall glorify me. Because by making you spiritual he will make clear how the Son is equal to the Father, whom they knew according to the flesh as a man, or by taking away fear he will make you proclaim my glory to the whole world, which profits not me but men. Of mine. Not that the Spirit is less than the Son. Why he said this, he explains: All things whatsoever the Father hath are mine. Therefore I said that he shall receive of mine. Therefore the Spirit receives from the Father, whence the Son receives, because in this Trinity the Son is born of the Father, the Spirit proceeds from the Father. But he who is born of none and proceeds from none is the Father alone.
16.15: 16.15 All things, etc. AUG. Christ speaks of the Spirit. The Spirit of the Father, etc., up to: thus it is clearly shown that the Spirit is of the Father and the Son.
16.16: 16.16 A little while. That is, a short time remains until I suffer and am shut in the sepulchre, and again a short time until you see me risen. Or the short time is the three days in which, shut in, I shall not be seen. And again a little while, that is, the forty days, in which I shall be seen risen. Because I go. That is, because it is time that, having laid aside mortality, I carry human nature to the heavens.
16.20: 16.20 That you shall lament. When I am killed, over which my enemies will rejoice. In like manner all the good weep amid the troubles of this world; but the lovers of the world rejoice. But the good are compared to a woman in labor who has given birth in her travail; but she rejoices over the fruit, and rejoices more over the coming of the future offspring than she is sad over the present pain.
16.23: 16.23 If you ask anything. AUG. What he says, he will give you, is surely to be understood so that it is known that the benefits signified are those which properly pertain to those who ask. For the saints are heard for themselves, but not for all others, friends or enemies. He will give you. In the future you will not ask, but now ask and it shall be given you what pertains to you, even if not to all those for whom you ask, and therefore it is said to you.
16.25: 16.25 These things in proverbs. What I have said so far I have said as in proverbs (which men are accustomed to hear but not understand), because you are animal men. But the animal man perceiveth not the things that are of the Spirit of God I John 1.. Whatever is said of the incorporeal and unchangeable substance has as it were the quality of proverbs. But the hour cometh. In which, the Spirit being given, I will make you spiritual, so that with the surest understanding of the mind (though not as in the future) you may see God, and then I will openly show you of the Father, that you may understand him and me to be of the same substance, and then, Ask in my name. Because then you will truly know and understand that if as man I ask the Father, as God I hear with the Father; hence he says: And I say not to you that I will ask the Father.
16.27: 16.27 For the Father himself. The Father loves us because we love the Son, since we have received from the Father and the Son that we love the Father and the Son: charity being given through the Spirit, whom also we love with the Father and the Son, the one who loves first makes in us what is loved.
16.28: 16.28 Again I leave the world. He left the world by bodily presence. He goeth to the Father, because he brought humanity to the invisible things of the Father's majesty. He left the world, because he took away from the sight of the lovers of the world what they had seen. He returns to his country, because he taught his lovers to believe him equal to the Father.
16.29: 16.29 His disciples say to him. When the hour which he promised had not yet come: Behold, now thou speakest plainly. The things which the Lord knows are proverbs to those who do not understand: they understand us so far that they do not even understand that they do not understand. Admonishing them of this weakness of theirs, he answered: Do you now believe, etc.
16.30: 16.30 Now we know that thou knowest all things. They openly show that, speaking of them, he dealt chiefly with those things which they were pleased to hear: and the things which they themselves wished to ask, he anticipated and brought forth of his own accord, and therefore, because he knew their thoughts, they confess that he knows all things, as God and the Son of God. And thou needest not, etc. Since you know all things, there is no need for you to question anyone from whom you may learn anything. Or even to be questioned by anyone, foreknowing what he wants. But if he ever asked or was asked, it was needful not for them, but for others.
16.31: 16.31 Do you now believe. As little ones, to whom whatever is lofty is still a proverb, you believe, but the hour of the passion cometh, and is now near, in which you will be so disturbed that what you now believe you will abandon, not only in body but also in the faith of the mind; hence: We hoped that it was he that should have redeemed Israel.
16.32: 16.32 And I am not, etc. Behold, they have advanced, but he wishes them to be stretched to something greater, so that when they have said: Thou camest forth from God, he says: The Father is with me, and they should not so think he came forth from God as to think he also withdrew. Because the Father is with me. He had said, I leave the world and go to the Father; now he says: The Father is with me, which is a word to him who understands, a proverb to him who does not. Though it is not food for him, yet it is nourishment of milk. From this it is that they knew that he knew all things.
17.1: 17.1 These things Jesus spoke. Not only what was said at the supper, but also what was said from the beginning. But chiefly what was said at the supper, he says were said for this cause, that they might have peace in him. This is the peace for which we are Christians, for which we are imbued with the sacraments, for which we are instructed in every way, for which we received the Spirit as a pledge, for which we believe in him and hope and are inflamed with love of him. This is consolation and deliverance in troubles. Father, the hour is come. He could have prayed in silence, but in praying he is also a teacher, and makes the prayer known as an edification of those present and those to come. The hour is come. Not by the pressure of fate, but by the ordering of God, who without time ordained all things that happen in time in fitting order. Glorify thy Son. Humility began in the passion, glory in the resurrection. The hour of the passion has come, of sowing humility; delay not the glory of the resurrection, that thy Son may glorify thee. And thus the glory of the Father can be neither increased nor diminished in itself. Among men it was less while he was known only in Judea, but through the resurrection of the Son he became known everywhere. That thy Son may glorify thee. In the knowledge of men, as thou hast given, so that they may know thee, and him whom thou hast sent. For the Father cannot be glorified in the knowledge of man unless he is known through whom he is glorified, that is, unless the people become acquainted with him, and this is the glorification of the Father, which is not about the apostles alone but about all believers.
17.3: 17.3 And this is, etc. The order: That they may know thee, and him whom thou hast sent, that is, Christ with the Spirit, who is of both, to be one and the only true God. If therefore the Son glorifies thee in the way thou hast given him power over all creation, and hast so given that all that thou hast given him he may give to them eternal life: And this is eternal life, that they may know thee. Thus the Son glorifies thee, that he may make thee known to all whom thou hast given him. That they may know thee. What is here from the Father will be full in the future. He, therefore, who advances in knowledge tends more to live. But when the knowledge will be full, there will be praise without end. And this is that glorification, but first here he is glorified while he becomes known to the faithful; hence: I have glorified thee on the earth.
17.4: 17.4 I have finished the work. That is, if he were saying openly of the future, I will glorify, by preaching to the nations. I will finish the work, because it is already done by predestination; and what is most certainly to be must be held as already done. This predestination he opens more manifestly in his glorification, saying: Which I had with thee before the world was; that is, as I then had in predestination with thee before the ages, so now in reality do in the world in time. Thou hast given me, etc. In which grace is noted. For he has nothing in man which he has not received.
17.5: 17.5 To men. All these things can be said of all the faithful to come. And this is the glorification by which the glorified Son glorifies the Father upon earth, according to what is past for future.
17.6: 17.6 They were thine. AUG. These were the Father's as all things, etc., up to: because man was not yet.
17.7: 17.7 They have known. Lest the knowledge be thought already accomplished by sight, he adds: They have believed truly; not in the manner in which, when he said: Do you now believe, the hour cometh that you shall be scattered. But neither were they yet such, but he foretells what they will be, the Spirit having been received, without whom they did not keep the word which he had spoken.
17.9: 17.9 I pray for them. The first prayer was: Glorify thy Son, that thy Son may glorify thee, and he carried this out about these and concluded in the faith of believers. Now he prays for them that the Father may keep those whom he himself has left in the body.
17.10: 17.10 And all my things. For the Father did not lose by giving to the Son, since the Son still adds: All my things are thine, and thine are mine. All things that are the Father's are the Only-begotten Son's, by the fact that he himself is also God, also born of the Father, and equal to the Father.
17.11: 17.11 Keep them. That they may be one in their own nature, as we also are one in ours; and therefore he does not say, that they may be one with us, or that they themselves and we may be one as we are one, because they are not of the same nature with God, as the Son, according as he is God, is one with the Father.
17.12: 17.12 While I was. We must not understand that the Father and the Son keep by turns, as though one after the other. For the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, who is one God, keep together. But Scripture does not raise us up unless it comes down to us. When it speaks thus, let us understand it to distinguish persons, not to separate nature. The joy which he expressed above, that they may be one as also [.....] this is that peace and blessedness in the future age, for the sake of which all things are done, for the sake of which he says he has spoken in the world.
17.17: 17.17 Sanctify. As by thy grace the sanctification has begun, by which they are now not of the world, by the same grace make them more holy, that they may persevere in the truth, of which the ancient sanctifications were a shadow; that is, in me who am the truth, which he opens by adding: Thy word is truth, which is, I am the truth. In Greek, in Latin word or speech, who is the only-begotten of the Father.
17.19: 17.19 And for them do I sanctify myself. That is, that it may profit them, I as man will sanctify myself in me, the Word, which is from the beginning of his Incarnation when the Word was made flesh. And thus it profits them, because I sanctify in myself also them, who are I, because the head and the body are one Christ; hence he adds: that they also may be as I am, sanctified in truth and in me.
17.20: 17.20 Not for them. Now he begins to speak not of the apostles alone or of the other members. But he does not pray for those who have already died in his faith, but for those who are in temptations. But for them also who. Until the end of the world, or who already believe wherever they are, though not so perfectly as those who after the resurrection are to believe. Through their word. Through the word of the Gospel, which is theirs, not that it was preached through them only, but also through Paul and any others, but because it was first and principally committed to them to preach. This is the word of faith, the word of God, through which the thief believed, Paul believed, and whoever believes.
17.21: 17.21 That they all may be one. He does not say, All are one, but that they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee, understand: are one: So also the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father, that they may be one, because they are of one substance. But we can be in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. Or the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit can be in us, yet we cannot be one with God, because we are not of one substance. But God is in us as in a temple, we in him as a creature in the Creator. That they also. He says in us, that what they are one in faith and charity they may attribute to the grace of God, as now, however, light in the Lord. That the world. The world here is taken for all those who are one. Nor does what they are cause them to believe, since rather by believing they are one; although they were one by nature, yet by dissenting from the one they were not one; but he said by praying that the world may believe, as by praying he said that all may be one, as though a third petition were understood: I ask that the world may believe.
17.24: 17.24 Whom thou hast given. That is, whom thou hast drawn to me, so I too have chosen them out of the world: others are not given to him, are not his, although the power over all is his. I will. What the Omnipotent wills cannot fail to be done, but that is the will of the man, of which he says: Not as I will Matth. 26.. That they may see. When in the form of the servant glorified they shall see him judging good and evil, the wicked man shall be taken away that he may not see the glory of God by which he is God, which the clean of heart alone shall see, and that will be to them eternal life.
17.26: 17.26 That the love. The love with which the Father loves the Son is in all the just, because they are his members and are loved in him who is wholly loved, therefore he adds: And I in them. As if to say: Because I am in them, he is in us in one way as in a temple, we in him in another; because we are he, since according to his humanity we are the body of the head.
18.1: 18.1 Where was. He is taken in a garden to blot out the sin committed in the garden of delights, into which, crossing the torrent of this world, he brought his disciples.
18.3: 18.3 A band. Not of Jews, but of soldiers from the governor, the order of lawful authority being kept, so that none would dare to resist those holding him; or even if anyone dared, he could not against so many. Cometh thither. He is betrayed by night, that he might be found without the crowds, which in the daytime were frequently present.
18.5: 18.5 I am he. With this one word, about to die, he laid low so many fierce and strong men by the power of the hidden Godhead: because he indeed wished to be seized, but not except when he willed.
18.6: 18.6 They went backward and fell to the ground. So now, through the Gospel everywhere Christ says, I am he, and the Jews, awaiting Antichrist, go backward and fall into earthly things, which they love.
18.8: 18.8 Let these go their way. AUG. They do what he commands, they let go those whom he does not wish to perish, not that they would not die afterward, but because they did not yet believe as they believe who do not perish.
18.11: 18.11 Put up. As if he were saying: Let vengeance be still. Otherwise: Turn the sword back to its place, that is, turn the word of preaching to the nations, where, according to Paul, a door great and wide is found open. Otherwise, after the fullness shall have entered, he says to Peter, through whom the whole order of preachers is designated: Send the word of preaching to Israel. For all that take the sword shall perish with the sword Matth. 26.. With what sword? With that which turns about, flaming, before paradise: and with the sword of the Spirit, which is written in the armor of God.
18.12: 18.12 Then the band. It was the custom of the Jews that whomever they judged worthy of death they handed over bound to the governor.
18.13: 18.13 And they led him. There were at that time two chief priests (as Luke says), Annas and Caiphas, who took turns in their years. But then it was the year of Caiphas, and by his will Jesus was led first to Annas, not because he was his colleague but because he was his father-in-law. Or the houses were so situated that Annas ought not to be passed by by those passing.
18.15: 18.15 And another disciple. Who this is, since it is not said here, let it not be rashly defined. Yet John is accustomed to indicate himself in this way.
18.17: 18.17 He saith: I am not. AUG. He denies Christ not only who says that he is not Christ, but also who denies that he is a Christian, and so is fulfilled what the Lord said: Thou shalt deny me thrice Matth. 26..
18.21: 18.21 Why askest thou me? That is, from whom you do not desire to hear the truth. Ask rather those about whose words you have no ill will. He so tempers the answer that he neither concealed the truth nor seemed to defend himself.
18.22: 18.22 And when he had said these things. It is objected: why did he not do what he taught? He ought not to have answered so, but to offer the other cheek. But he answered truthfully and meekly and justly, and prepared for the one striking not only his cheek but his whole body. And from this he rather shows that the precepts of patience are to be fulfilled not by display of the body, but by the preparation of the heart, for one can offer the cheek visibly while angry. It is better, therefore, that he answers truly, being truly appeased, and prepared to bear graver things with a tranquil mind.
18.23: 18.23 If I have spoken evil. He speaks evil who speaks against the truth. If I have spoken evil, give testimony by which you may prove me a liar.
18.25: 18.25 And Simon Peter. AUG. Having said that Annas sent Jesus to Caiphas, he returns to the place in the narrative where he had left Peter, to explain what had happened in the house of Annas concerning Peter's threefold denial.
18.28: 18.28 Into the hall of judgment. That is, where the governor Pilate lived. But if to Caiphas, how into the hall of judgment? Perhaps, some cause urging, both had come together from the house of Annas to hear Jesus. Caiphas went on to the governor's hall, and left Jesus with his father-in-law to be heard; or Pilate had taken a hall in the house of Caiphas, and the house was so large that the master lived in one part, Pilate in another. That they might not be defiled. Because in the days of the unleavened bread it was a defilement to them to enter the dwelling of a foreigner.
18.31: 18.31 It is not lawful for us, etc. They say this because of the holiness of the feast day. For the law commands that they spare not evildoers, especially those who seduce from their God, such as they said this man was; and they speak against themselves, because they were killing him whom they were offering to be killed, as Pilate also killed him, though not with his own hands. When Pilate wished to hand Jesus over to the Jews, that they might judge him according to their law, they refused to receive him, saying: It is not lawful for us to put any man to death; and thus the word of Jesus is fulfilled which he foretold of his death, that being handed over by the Jews, the Gentiles would kill him, as if those who sin more were thus strangers to the crime, in which not their innocence but their madness is shown.
18.34: 18.34 Sayest thou this thing of thyself, etc. Jesus knows what he himself asks and what the other is going to answer, but yet he willed it to be said, not that he might know, but that what he willed to know might be written.
18.35: 18.35 What hast thou done. As if: If this is not a fault, that you have called yourself a king, what else have you done? As though it is no wonder if you are handed over to the judge to be punished, you who call yourself a king. But if this were not the cause, then perhaps another would have to be sought; as if: confirm whether this is the cause that is charged, or another.
18.36: 18.36 Kingdom. This is what he wished us to know, but first, by questioning in turn, he wished to show what was the opinion of men about his kingdom, of Jews or Gentiles, and this being shown he answers both more aptly: My kingdom is not of this world. As if: You are deceived; for I do not hinder your dominion in this world, that you may not fear in vain and serve, but I would have you come to the heavenly kingdom by believing.
18.37: 18.37 Thou sayest. He is not afraid to confess himself king, but is so free that he neither denies he is king nor confesses he is of the world, as that man supposed who said: Art thou a king then? To whom he answered: Thou sayest that I am a king. As if to say: Carnal, you speak carnally.
18.38: 18.38 Again. He does not wait for an answer, lest delay occur when he wished to release him, for suddenly the custom came to his mind by which one could be released at the Pasch.
18.39: 18.39 But you have. Because at the Pasch they were freed from slavery, at the Pasch this custom of releasing someone for them arose.
18.40: 18.40 Now Barabbas was a robber. That is, son of the master, that is, of the devil, who was master in perfidy to the robber in his crime among the Jews. Or Barabbas, that is, son of the father, that is, of the devil.
19.1: 19.1 Then therefore. Pilate did this, that is, he allowed the soldiers to do it, or even ordered it, so that the Jews, satisfied with the punishments, might desist from his death.
19.2: 19.2 They put a crown of thorns upon his head. In the crown of thorns the taking up of our sins is signified, for which he willed to become mortal. Hence the forerunner: Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world. For thorns are used to signify sins. Hence the Lord: The earth shall bring forth to thee thorns and thistles Gen. 3.. That is, thy conscience will not cease to produce pricks and stings of vices.
19.4: 19.4 Pilate therefore went forth. Behold, what Jesus had foretold of himself is fulfilled by hidden power; the patience by which martyrs are formed is commended.
19.5: 19.5 And he saith to them. Here it appears that Pilate was not ignorant that these things were done by the soldiers, whether he ordered or permitted them, so that, the Jews being satisfied, these might suffice; but they burn the more and cry out: Crucify him, crucify him.
19.7: 19.7 The Son of God. Behold another, greater envy, because the unlawful claim to a kingdom seemed small, and yet he was truly both, Christ, both king and Son of God.
19.9: 19.9 But Jesus. Here and in other places we read that Christ was silent so that the prophecy might be fulfilled: As a lamb before the shearer, without voice, so he opened not his mouth Isa. 53.. This likeness is given from the lamb, that in his silence he may be held not guilty but innocent. For he is not convicted as one conscious of guilt, but is sacrificed as a meek one for others.
19.12: 19.12 And from henceforth. That is, from this cause, lest he have the sin of killing an innocent man (even if less than they, the envious), he sought to release him, not that he then first sought it, but if he wished it before, now he sought it. If thou release this man, thou art not Caesar's friend. They put forward the law first, according to which he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God: but because he does not fear the law of a foreign nation, but fears rather to kill the Son of God, they frighten him with Caesar, whom he cannot despise as the author of his power.
19.14: 19.14 And it was the Parasceve. AUG. Parasceve, which is interpreted preparation, etc., up to: and the same is the sixth hour of the preparation.
19.15: 19.15 Shall I crucify your king? Still he tries to overcome the terror which they bring in about Caesar, saying: Shall I crucify your king? Wishing to break them by their own disgrace, whom he could not soften by the disgrace of Christ.
19.16: 19.16 Then therefore. Because they openly profess that Caesar is against him if he wishes to impose another king on them by releasing unpunished one whom they had handed over to be killed for these boldnesses. Conquered therefore by fear, he delivered Jesus to them to be crucified. He delivered Jesus to them to be crucified. To them, not that they themselves received him with their hands, who had excused themselves from this, but that they might seem implicated in the crime from which they strive to be free, though Pilate did this only for them, hence he does not say that they should crucify, but that he should be crucified by the judgment and power of Pilate.
19.17: 19.17 Bearing. Jesus carried his own cross. A great mockery to the wicked, a great mystery to the pious who glory, as in the sceptre of a kingdom, and the cross is the lampstand of the lamp which was not to be put under a bushel. First the Lord carries the cross, because he suffered first; afterward it was laid on Simon of Cyrene, because we ought to follow his steps.
19.18: 19.18 And with him. The robber who remained in perfidy signifies the Jews; he who confesses signifies the Gentiles.
19.19: 19.19 And it was written. These three languages excelled the others: Hebrew because of the Jews, who glory in the law of God; Greek because of the wise of the nations; Latin because of the Romans, who then ruled almost all nations.
19.23: 19.23 The soldiers therefore, when they had crucified him. Behold what was done beside the cross, when he was already crucified. Four. The garment divided in four signifies the Church spread through the whole world, which consists of four parts, distributed equally to all parts, that is, harmoniously. The tunic obtained by lot, for all parts, signifies unity, which is held by the bond of charity. From the top. Because charity stands above all through the whole, since no one is without it who seems to belong to the whole, from which whole, as the Greek language shows, the Church is called catholic, which is commended in the lot by the grace of God.
19.26: 19.26 When Jesus therefore had seen his mother and the disciple standing whom he loved. He who was about to do divine things, as it were put aside his mother as unknown; now he shows that the hour had come, of which he then spoke, in which he acknowledges her of whom he was born mortally. And he teaches that care be given to parents by pious children, hence also the Apostle: If any man have not care of his own, he hath denied the faith I Tim. 5., etc.
19.27: 19.27 And from that hour the disciple took her. Who, although he now had nothing of his own, in that society had received a hundredfold, where all things were common, having nothing and possessing all things.
20.4: 20.4 And they both ran. John signifies the Synagogue, which came first to the sepulchre but did not enter, because it heard the prophecies about the incarnation and passion, but did not wish to believe in him as dead. Peter signifies the Church, which knew him dead in the flesh, believed him living God, after whom also in Judea at the end it will enter.
20.7: 20.7 Wrapped up. Because the sacraments of the Divinity are incomprehensible and removed from the knowledge of our weakness. In the wrapped-up cloth neither end nor beginning is seen. So the loftiness of the Divinity neither began to be nor ceases. Into one place. Because God is not in the tearing apart of minds, but in unity. Or, the napkin of the head is the passion of Christ, whose sacraments are hidden from unbelievers apart, because far from ours, since he suffered willingly and without fault, we unwillingly and with fault.
20.9: 20.9 For as yet. Namely, so far that, although it was openly said by the Lord himself, because of their habit of hearing parables from him, they did not understand.
20.11: 20.11 Weeping. Now she weeps more over the one taken away than over the one slain, because of so great a master whose life had been taken away not even a memory remained, and this grief held her there. While therefore, etc. Though she knew he was not there, yet because she grieves too much, she trusted neither her own eyes nor the eyes of those two who believed. Or rather this was done by divine instinct.
20.12: 20.12 She saw two. Angels, that is, messengers, signify that the Gospel of Christ is to be announced from head to feet, that is, from the beginning to the end. And he was to be announced from his passion, because he is God before the ages, and man at the end of the age. The angel therefore sits at the head when he says: In the beginning was the Word. At the feet when he says: The Word was made flesh. Or the two angels are the two Testaments, one earlier, the other following. Joined together, they announce with one mind that he was incarnate, died, and rose.
20.13: 20.13 Woman, why weepest thou? As if to say: Do not sin. They in a way forbid tears by announcing joy. But she, thinking they were asking in ignorance, reveals the cause of her tears: Because they have taken away my Lord, that is, the body of my Lord.
20.14: 20.14 And she knew not that it was Jesus, etc. Because she had her back to him whom she did not believe to have risen; because she loved and doubted, saw and did not recognize.
20.15: 20.15 Whom seekest thou? She, thinking that he was the gardener, saith to him. Not that she doubted whom she was seeking, but because she does not know the one she seeks, for she does not seek Christ, but the one she thinks was snatched away. Sir. She calls Lord the one she thinks the gardener, to honor the man from whom she was asking a favor. Nor does she call him Lord in the way she does the one she seeks as taken away. But recognizing Jesus she calls him Master, because she recalls him from whom she was learning to discern human and divine things. If thou hast taken him hence. She does not say whom, because the force of love does this in the mind, that she believes no one else ignorant of him of whom she always thinks.
20.16: 20.16 Mary. Turning, she saith to him: Rabboni, which is to say, Master. Jesus saith to her. After he called with a common name and was not recognized, he calls by name, as if to say, Recognize him by whom you are recognized.
20.18: 20.18 Mary Magdalene cometh, telling the disciples, that she had seen the Lord, etc. There the fault is cut off from where it proceeded. A woman gave death to a man to drink; now a woman announces life to men, and she who then told the words of the serpent now tells the words of the life-giver, as if God were saying by the very events: From the hand by which the drink of death was brought, receive the drink of life.
20.19: 20.19 When it was late, etc. This was done on the very day of the resurrection, on which Jesus appeared five times. First to Mary Magdalene, second to the same with others running to tell the disciples, third to Peter, fourth to Cleophas and his companion, fifth to the disciples with the doors shut, the two aforesaid having already returned.
20.20: 20.20 He shewed them his hands and his side. After the resurrection the Lord showed two opposite things in his body, both the palpable, of the same nature, to form them to faith, and the incorruptible, of another glory, to invite them to the reward.
20.21: 20.21 He said therefore to them again. Peace be to you, etc. He offers peace who came for the sake of peace, he repeats it to show that through his blood the things that are in heaven and the things that are on earth have been pacified.
20.22: 20.22 Receive ye the Holy Spirit. AUG. On earth the Spirit is given that the neighbor may be loved, from heaven the Spirit is given that God may be loved.
20.23: 20.23 Whose sins you shall forgive. Behold charity, which is poured into their hearts through the Holy Spirit. He forgives the sins of those who are partakers of it; of those who are not, he retains. And therefore after he said: Receive ye the Holy Spirit, he immediately added: Whose sins you shall forgive.
20.24: 20.24 But Thomas, one. Not by chance, but by divine arrangement Thomas was absent and did not believe what he heard; hence the Lord offered himself to be touched by him, because by his doubt and the proof made to him there is left to no one now any doubting. Who is called Didymus. Didymus, that is twin, because Thomas was doubtful, that is, an abyss: because by doubting he came to know more deeply.
20.28: 20.28 Answered. He saw and touched the man, and beyond this believed God, doubt being now removed, and confessed him whom he did not see.
20.29: 20.29 Because thou hast seen me, Thomas, thou hast believed. He does not say, you have touched, but you have seen: because sight is in a way the general sense, which is wont to be said of the other four. Perhaps he did not dare to touch; but by looking only, or also by touching, he believes. Blessed. He commends the faith of the Gentiles, but uses the past tense, as one who knew in his predestination as already done what was to be.
21.1: 21.1 Afterwards he manifested. They had followed Jesus, leaving all things. If after the death of Jesus, before he was restored to them alive, they had gone back to their former trade, they might seem to have done so out of despair; but after he was restored alive, after receiving the spirit of his breathing upon them, after his words: As the Father hath sent me, I also send you, suddenly they become what they had been, fishermen, not of men but of fish. But it must be known that they were not forbidden to seek a living by their lawful craft, the integrity of the apostolate being preserved, since they had nothing to live on, and so, as they labored, God added the necessaries which he promised, but here their want was arranged so that in the fishing so great sacraments might be displayed.
21.14: 21.14 This is now. Not that he was manifested only three times, but he refers it by days: the first day on which he rose, after eight days, this day when he did this about the fishes. The manifestations are therefore numbered by days. The first, however many times it was made, on one day, the day of the resurrection. The second, after eight days, and this is the third. With this third manifestation this Gospel ends.
21.15: 21.15 When therefore they had dined. Jesus knows what he asks when he asks whether he loves more, Peter says what he knows of himself, that is, that he loves. And because he does not know how much others love, therefore he is silent as to whether he loves more than they. Behold, he teaches not to define rashly about hidden things, and in view of the former danger of denial he answered more cautiously about himself. Feed my lambs. If you love me, feed my lambs. Not as your own: seek my glory in them, not yours; my gains, not yours, because the love of God is proved in the love of neighbor. But he who denies the work of piety to his neighbors loves God less. But this charity is given from divine grace. This John tacitly hints when, in questioning about love, he says here what he does not elsewhere: Simon son of John, that is, obedient by the grace of God, because that he loves and obeys more ardently than the others is nothing but the grace of God.
21.17: 21.17 He said to him the third time. He asks what he knew, not once but again and a third time; and a third time he hears from Peter that he is loved, and a third time he bids him feed the sheep. To the threefold denial a threefold confession is given in return, lest the tongue serve love less than fear. And as it was the judgment of fear to deny the shepherd, so it is the office of love to feed the Lord's flock. Peter was grieved. AUG. Even when sins are forgiven man endures misery, into which he came through sin. For the punishment is longer than the fault, nor would the fault seem small if the punishment were taken away with it. Therefore, whether to demonstrate the misery that is owed, or to amend a slippery life, or to exercise necessary patience, punishment holds man for a time, even him whom the fault no longer holds guilty, and this is the condition of these days, to be lamented, but not to be censured. Feed. To feed the sheep is to strengthen believers lest they fail, to provide earthly aids for subjects if necessary, to give examples of virtues, to resist adversaries, to correct sinners.
21.18: 21.18 But when thou shalt be old. He who had foretold the denial now foretells the suffering; by now he could do it, strengthened by the resurrection, what in his weakness he had promised prematurely. Now he does not fear the loss of this life, because with the Lord rising the example of another life has gone before.
21.19: 21.19 And when he had said this. These words having been said, Jesus began to go away, and Peter, not yet understanding what he had heard, Follow me, began to follow with his steps, and John followed too, who knew that he was loved.
21.20: 21.20 Whom Jesus loved. He loved others too, but this one he endowed more familiarly with a greater sweetness of his love, because, chosen a virgin by him, he remained a virgin, hence he also commended his mother to him. AUG. By the name being left unspoken John is distinguished from the others, etc., up to: that John, who is a virgin, agrees with the future life, where they shall neither marry nor be married. Upon his breast. In the breast of Jesus are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden, upon which he leaned whom he endows with a greater and singular gift of wisdom and knowledge than the rest, in which was prefigured how great secrets of the divinity he, beyond the others, was to write.
21.21: 21.21 Lord, and what shall this man do? Because Peter had heard that he was to be crucified, he wished also to know the end of his brother.
21.22: 21.22 So I will have him remain till I come. I do not wish him to finish through martyrdom, but to await the peaceful release of his flesh, when I, coming, shall receive him into eternal blessedness.
21.23: 21.23 And he did not say to him. It is not to be understood that John did not die in the flesh, but that whatever he suffered before, a final old age in peace would end it. For it was not a great thing to give the beloved not to die, since to be dissolved and to be with Christ is much better.
21.24: 21.24 This is, etc. Here he openly designates his own person by his office, which he did not wish to designate by his name.
21.25: 21.25 I think that the world itself. AUG. It is not to be believed that the world cannot contain by space of places, etc., up to: like other tropes, that is, modes of speech. Nor the world itself. He does not say that it cannot be contained by space, but by the capacity of readers, although, the faith of the matters being preserved, words very often seem to exceed belief by hyperbole.
